lessons.title: Start here
lessons.html:
This course takes you from a naive FP32 model running in a Python loop to a globally deployed, autoscaled, multi-tenant LLM service. It has five parts:

  1. Foundations - the systems knowledge every later lab leans on: how a GPU executes work, why decode is memory-bound, what the KV cache costs, how GPUs talk to each other, how CUDA launches work, number formats, HTTP streaming, containers, Kubernetes, and how to measure latency properly.
  2. Engine labs - make one model server fast, twice, with two engines:
    • vLLM track (labs/, 12 labs): FP32 baseline, precision, continuous batching and paged KV cache, attention backends (FlashAttention 4, FlashInfer, Triton), prefix caching, chunked prefill, CUDA graphs and compilation levels, INT4 AWQ/GPTQ, FP8/MXFP8/MXFP4, speculative decoding (draft model, EAGLE-3, n-gram), tensor parallelism, capstone.
    • SGLang track (sglang/, 14 labs): the same journey in SGLang plus RadixAttention, the overlap scheduler, structured output, MoE expert parallelism, attention backends and HiCache.
  3. Fleet labs - the llm-d track (llmd/, 10 labs): inference-aware routing (EPP), scorer design, flow control, tiered KV cache, prefill/ decode disaggregation, wide expert parallelism, then the upstream Kubernetes guides and autoscaling.
  4. Cloud & global deployment - regions, DNS and anycast, edge and gateways, capacity and cost, reliability and security.
  5. How it fits together - one request's life from DNS to GPU and back, a reference architecture, and a symptom-to-fix optimization playbook.

Hardware assumed

One node with 8x NVIDIA B200 (Blackwell, SM100, ~180 GB HBM3e each, NVLink 5 through NVSwitch), CUDA 13, Python 3.11, vLLM 0.26+ in a conda env for the vLLM track, a separate sglang-labs env for SGLang, and Docker (+ minikube for the Kubernetes labs) for llm-d.

Suggested order

Week Read Do
1 Foundations 1-4 vLLM labs 00-06
2 Foundations 5-8 vLLM labs 07-11, SGLang labs 00-07
3 How it fits together 1 (request lifecycle) SGLang labs 08-13, llm-d labs 00-03
4 Cloud 1-5, How it fits together 2-3 llm-d labs 04-09

Using the app

Every module and lab README is a lesson. Modules end with flashcards: use Learn to flip through them and Test to quiz yourself; cards you mark Review come back first. On a phone, swipe left/ right to move between cards. Your progress is stored on the device.

lessons.title: GPU architecture for inference
lessons.html:
The parts that matter

A GPU is a large array of streaming multiprocessors (SMs) sharing a pool of high-bandwidth memory.

            ┌────────────── GPU (B200: two dies, one logical GPU) ──────────────┐
            │  SM  SM  SM  SM  ... (~148 SMs)                                   │
            │  each SM: 4 warp schedulers, CUDA cores, 5th-gen tensor cores,     │
            │           registers, shared memory / L1 (~228 KB), TMEM (256 KB)   │
            │                         L2 cache (~126 MB total)                   │
            │                HBM3e: ~180 GB @ ~8 TB/s                            │
            └────────────────────── NVLink 5: 1.8 TB/s ──────────────────────────┘
  • Threads run in warps of 32; a warp executes one instruction for all 32 threads at once (SIMT). Blocks of warps are scheduled onto SMs.
  • Tensor cores do small matrix multiply-accumulates per instruction. They are where almost all LLM FLOPs happen. Blackwell's 5th-generation tensor cores add FP4/FP6 and microscaling (MX) formats, keep accumulators in a dedicated tensor memory (TMEM), and can pair two SMs on one MMA.
  • Memory hierarchy: registers → shared memory/L1 (per SM, ~tens of TB/s) → L2 (shared) → HBM (~8 TB/s on B200) → host DRAM over PCIe Gen5/C2C (~64-450 GB/s) → NVMe/network.

Approximate B200 peak numbers (dense, no sparsity):

Format Tensor-core throughput
BF16 / FP16 ~2.2 PFLOP/s
FP8 ~4.5 PFLOP/s
FP4 (NVFP4/MXFP4) ~9 PFLOP/s
FP32 (non-tensor) ~80 TFLOP/s

The FP32 row is why lab 00's FP32 baseline is so slow: FP32 matmuls can't use the fast tensor-core paths at all (TF32 can, at reduced precision).

The roofline model

Every kernel needs some FLOPs and moves some bytes. Its arithmetic intensity is FLOPs / bytes. The GPU's ridge point is peak FLOP/s / peak bytes/s:

ridge = 2.2e15 FLOP/s ÷ 8e12 B/s ≈ 280 FLOP/byte   (BF16)
  • Intensity below the ridge → memory-bound: time = bytes / bandwidth. Faster math doesn't help; moving fewer bytes does (quantization, caching, fusion).
  • Intensity above the ridge → compute-bound: time = FLOPs / peak. Lower-precision tensor cores and better kernels help.

Why decode is memory-bound

For a linear layer with a d × d BF16 weight matrix and a batch of B tokens: FLOPs = 2·B·d², bytes (weights dominate) ≈ 2·d². Intensity ≈ B FLOP/byte.

  • Decode processes one new token per sequence per step, so B = number of running sequences (often 1-256) - far below 280. Each step must stream all the weights from HBM. Lower bound for an 8B BF16 model: 16 GB / 8 TB/s ≈ 2 ms per step, whatever the batch size up to the ridge. That is why batching many sequences is nearly free throughput.
  • Prefill processes the whole prompt at once: B = thousands of tokens → compute-bound.

Attention during decode is even more memory-bound: each sequence reads its entire KV cache for one query token, and that cannot be shared across the batch.

Occupancy, launch overhead, and small batches

A kernel launch costs a few microseconds of CPU time. A decode step for a 32-layer model launches hundreds of kernels; at small batch the GPU work per kernel can be shorter than the launch cost, so the GPU idles waiting for the CPU. CUDA graphs (vLLM lab 06, SGLang lab 07) record the launch sequence once and replay it in one call.

lessons.title: Transformer inference and the KV cache
lessons.html:
One forward pass

A decoder-only transformer turns token ids into embeddings, runs them through L identical layers, and projects the last hidden state to vocabulary logits:

tokens → embed → [ RMSNorm → Attention(Q,K,V) → + → RMSNorm → MLP / MoE → + ] × L → norm → LM head → logits → sample
  • Attention mixes information across positions: each token's query Q is compared with the keys K of all earlier tokens, and the softmax-weighted values V are summed.
  • MLP (or MoE: a router picks k of E expert MLPs per token) is where most parameters and FLOPs live.

Prefill and decode

Generation has two phases with opposite performance profiles:

Prefill Decode
Input per step the whole prompt (N tokens) 1 new token per sequence
Bound by compute (big matmuls) memory bandwidth (weights + KV)
Sets TTFT (time to first token) TPOT / ITL (time per output token)
Scales with prompt length (attention: ~N²) batch size, context length

The KV cache

Attention at step t needs K and V for every earlier token. Rather than recompute them, engines store them: the KV cache. Its size per token is

bytes/token = 2 × layers × kv_heads × head_dim × bytes_per_element

(2 for K and V). Examples in BF16:

Model L KV heads head dim KV per token 8K-token sequence
Llama-3.1-8B 32 8 128 128 KiB 1 GiB
Qwen2.5-7B 28 4 128 56 KiB 448 MiB
Qwen3-32B 64 8 128 256 KiB 2 GiB

So after weights, KV cache is what limits how many sequences you can run at once, and therefore throughput. Every major serving optimization touches it:

  • Paged KV cache (vLLM lab 02): store KV in fixed-size blocks (pages) allocated on demand, like virtual memory, instead of one contiguous slab per sequence sized for the max length. Near-zero fragmentation means far more concurrent sequences.
  • Prefix caching / RadixAttention (vLLM lab 04, SGLang lab 05): blocks are content-addressed by the tokens they hold, so requests that share a prefix (system prompt, document, conversation history) reuse them and skip that part of prefill.
  • KV quantization (FP8 KV, vLLM lab 08): half the bytes per token.
  • Offloading / tiering (SGLang lab 13, llm-d lab 04): spill KV to CPU RAM or disk instead of dropping it.
  • Prefix-aware routing (llm-d labs 01-02): send each request to the replica that already holds its prefix.
  • P/D disaggregation (llm-d lab 05): compute KV on prefill GPUs, ship it to decode GPUs.

Attention variants that shrink KV

  • MHA: one KV head per query head. GQA (Llama 3, Qwen): groups of query heads share a KV head (8 KV heads for 32-64 query heads) → 4-8x smaller KV. MQA: a single KV head.
  • MLA (DeepSeek-V2/V3): compresses K/V into a low-rank latent vector per token, decompressed inside the attention kernel - very small KV, needs special kernels (FlashMLA, TRT-LLM MLA).
  • Sliding-window / hybrid layers keep only recent tokens in some layers.

Continuous batching

Static batching waits for a batch of requests and runs them to completion, so short requests wait for the longest one. Continuous (iteration-level) batching re-forms the batch every step: finished sequences leave, waiting ones join (their prefill is scheduled into the step). All modern engines do this; it is the single biggest throughput win over a naive loop (vLLM lab 02).

Sampling

Logits → temperature/top-p/top-k → token. Greedy (temperature 0) is deterministic given identical numerics. Structured output (SGLang lab 09) masks logits so only tokens valid under a JSON schema/grammar can be sampled. Speculative decoding (vLLM lab 09, SGLang lab 08) drafts several tokens cheaply and verifies them in one target-model pass.

lessons.title: Interconnects, collectives and parallelism
lessons.html:
How GPUs talk

Link Typical bandwidth Where
NVLink 5 (B200) 1.8 TB/s per GPU (bidirectional) GPU↔GPU inside a node, via NVSwitch (all-to-all, non-blocking)
PCIe Gen5 x16 ~64 GB/s per direction GPU↔CPU, GPU↔NIC, NVMe
Grace C2C (GB200) ~900 GB/s GPU↔CPU on Grace-Blackwell
InfiniBand NDR / XDR 400 / 800 Gb/s per NIC (50 / 100 GB/s) node↔node, RDMA
RoCE v2 / AWS EFA 100-400 Gb/s per NIC node↔node, RDMA over Ethernet
Datacenter TCP 25-100 Gb/s everything else

Inside an 8-GPU HGX node every GPU reaches every other at full NVLink bandwidth through NVSwitch. Between nodes the bandwidth drops by an order of magnitude, so parallelism that needs a collective every layer stays inside the node.

RDMA (remote direct memory access) lets a NIC read/write remote memory without involving the remote CPU; GPUDirect RDMA lets it read GPU memory directly. That is how NIXL ships KV cache between prefill and decode pods (llm-d lab 05), and how NCCL runs collectives across nodes.

Collectives (NCCL)

Collective What it does Used by
all-reduce every rank ends with the sum of everyone's tensor tensor parallelism (after attention and MLP)
all-gather every rank ends with everyone's shards concatenated TP/sequence parallel, FSDP
reduce-scatter sum, then each rank keeps one shard TP variants, FSDP
all-to-all each rank sends a different chunk to each other rank expert parallelism (dispatch/combine)
send/recv point-to-point pipeline parallelism, KV transfer

A ring all-reduce moves about 2·(N−1)/N × the tensor size per GPU; on NVLink that's microseconds for decode-sized activations, but it happens twice per layer, so it adds up.

The parallelism menu

  • Tensor parallelism (TP): split each weight matrix across GPUs (column-parallel then row-parallel) so each GPU holds 1/N of every layer. Two all-reduces per layer. Cuts per-GPU weight memory and per-token latency; scales well inside NVLink, poorly across nodes. (vLLM lab 10, SGLang lab 04.)
  • Pipeline parallelism (PP): split layers into stages on different GPUs/nodes; activations flow stage to stage. Little communication, but bubbles unless many micro-batches are in flight. Used to span nodes.
  • Data parallelism (DP): independent replicas, each with full weights, serving different requests. No communication; this is what a fleet behind a router is. DP attention (SGLang lab 10, vLLM --data-parallel-size) runs attention data-parallel inside one MoE deployment.
  • Expert parallelism (EP): place whole MoE experts on different GPUs; route tokens to their experts with all-to-all. Wide EP spreads experts over dozens of GPUs (llm-d lab 06) using DeepEP kernels.
  • Context / sequence parallelism (CP): split one long sequence's tokens across GPUs for prefill of very long contexts.

Rule of thumb for serving: use the smallest TP that fits the model with enough KV headroom, then add DP replicas behind a router. TP beyond that buys latency, not throughput per GPU.

cards.a: TP needs two all-reduces per layer; NVLink/NVSwitch gives ~1.8 TB/s per GPU inside a node, but inter-node links are ~10x slower, so cross-node TP is communication-bound.

lessons.title: CUDA execution, kernels and compilation
lessons.html:
Host and device

Python/PyTorch runs on the host (CPU) and enqueues work onto CUDA streams; the device executes kernels from each stream in order, asynchronously. The CPU only waits when it needs a result (.item(), .cpu(), synchronize). An inference engine is mostly a CPU-side scheduler that keeps the GPU's queue full.

CPU: schedule batch ─ prepare inputs ─ launch k1 k2 k3 ... k800 ─ sample ─ detokenize ─ schedule next
GPU:                                   ███ ███ ███ ...  ███
                                       (gaps = GPU idle waiting for launches)

Engines hide CPU work with:

  • CUDA graphs: capture a whole forward pass for a fixed batch shape and replay it with one launch. vLLM captures graphs for a set of batch sizes (cudagraph_capture_sizes) and pads batches up to the next size. PIECEWISE graphs leave attention outside the graph; FULL graphs include it (needs graph-safe attention metadata).
  • Overlap / async scheduling: prepare step N+1 on the CPU while step N runs on the GPU (SGLang's overlap scheduler, lab 06; vLLM async scheduling).
  • Multi-process design: API server, tokenizer/detokenizer and engine core in separate processes so Python HTTP handling doesn't stall the GPU.

Kernels that matter

  • GEMMs (cuBLAS, CUTLASS, DeepGEMM, FlashInfer/TRT-LLM kernels): linear layers and expert MLPs. Quantized variants (FP8, MXFP4, INT4 AWQ/ Marlin) dequantize in registers.
  • Attention kernels: FlashAttention tiles Q/K/V through shared memory so the N×N score matrix never hits HBM; FA3 targets Hopper (TMA, warp specialization), FA4 targets Blackwell (CuTe-DSL, TMEM, 2-CTA MMA). FlashInfer and TRT-LLM provide paged-KV decode kernels. MLA models use FlashMLA / TRT-LLM MLA.
  • Fused small ops: RMSNorm + quantize, SiLU-and-mul, rotary embedding, residual add, all-reduce + norm. Each fusion removes an HBM round trip.
  • MoE: routing (top-k), permute/unpermute, grouped GEMM, all-to-all (DeepEP, pplx, NCCL).

torch.compile and Triton

torch.compile traces the model into an FX graph, and Inductor generates fused Triton kernels for the pointwise and reduction parts. vLLM wraps this as optimization levels -O0…-O3 plus custom fusion passes and caches the compiled artifacts (~/.cache/vllm/torch_compile_cache), so later startups skip compilation. Triton is a Python DSL for writing GPU kernels at the block level; it is portable across NVIDIA/AMD and is the fallback attention backend in both engines.

Startup cost

Model load + torch.compile + CUDA graph capture can take tens of seconds to minutes. Serving systems care because it determines how fast autoscaling can add capacity (llm-d lab 09): --enforce-eager starts fastest but runs slowest; compile caches, pre-captured graphs and sleep/wake (keeping weights in host memory) make cold starts warm.

lessons.title: Number formats and quantization
lessons.html:
Floating-point formats

Format Bits (sign/exp/mantissa) Range Notes
FP32 1/8/23 ±3.4e38 training master weights; no tensor-core fast path
TF32 1/8/10 FP32 range tensor-core FP32 "lite"
BF16 1/8/7 FP32 range default for inference; no overflow surprises
FP16 1/5/10 ±65504 more precision, can overflow activations
FP8 E4M3 1/4/3 ±448 weights/activations/KV
FP8 E5M2 1/5/2 ±57344 gradients; KV option
FP6 / FP4 E2M1 1/3/2, 1/2/1 tiny needs fine-grained scales

Halving bits halves weight bytes, which (decode being memory-bound) nearly halves decode step time, and lets more KV cache fit.

Scaling: why FP8/FP4 work

Low-bit formats have little range, so values are stored as q × scale. The question is how many values share one scale:

  • Per-tensor: one scale for the whole matrix. Simple; outliers hurt.
  • Per-channel / per-token: one scale per output channel (weights) or per token (activations).
  • Per-block: one scale per 128×128 weight block and 1×128 activation block (DeepSeek-V3 style, vLLM fp8_per_block).
  • Microscaling (MX): an 8-bit power-of-two scale (E8M0) per 32 elements: MXFP8, MXFP6, MXFP4 (OCP standard). NVIDIA's NVFP4 uses an FP8 scale per 16 elements plus a per-tensor scale. Blackwell tensor cores apply these block scales in hardware.

Weight-only vs weight-and-activation

  • Weight-only (W4A16, e.g. AWQ, GPTQ): weights stored in INT4, dequantized to BF16 in the kernel (Marlin). Cuts memory traffic; math stays BF16. Great for memory-bound decode at small batch.
  • W8A8 FP8: weights and activations in FP8; matmuls run on FP8 tensor cores (2x BF16 FLOPs). Helps both prefill (compute) and decode (bytes).
  • W4A4 (NVFP4/MXFP4): 4x fewer bytes than BF16 and FP4 tensor cores; needs good calibration or quantization-aware training to keep accuracy.

Offline vs online

  • Online / dynamic (vLLM --quantization fp8_per_tensor|fp8_per_block| mxfp8|mxfp4): quantize BF16 weights at load time; activation scales computed on the fly. No calibration data.
  • Offline / calibrated (AWQ, GPTQ, llm-compressor, ModelOpt): run calibration data through the model, pick scales (or rotate/smooth outliers), save a quantized checkpoint. Better accuracy at 4 bits.

KV-cache quantization

--kv-cache-dtype fp8_e4m3 stores K/V in FP8 with per-tensor or per-head scales: half the KV bytes → ~2x the concurrent tokens. Attention backends with native FP8 KV (FlashInfer/TRT-LLM on Blackwell) avoid a dequantize pass. Sensitive layers can be skipped (--kv-cache-dtype-skip-layers).

Always measure quality

Quantization is a throughput/quality trade: check perplexity or task accuracy (e.g. GSM8K, MMLU via lm-eval) for each scheme, not just tokens/s.

lessons.title: Processes, networking and the serving API
lessons.html:
Linux processes for servers

  • A server is a process listening on a TCP port (vLLM 8000, SGLang 30000, Envoy 8081). ss -ltnp shows who listens where; a port can only be bound by one process per address.
  • Engines spawn child processes (engine core, TP workers, tokenizer). Killing only the parent can leave orphans holding GPU memory - the labs start servers in their own process group (setsid) and kill the group (SIGTERM, then SIGKILL).
  • Signals: SIGTERM asks for graceful shutdown (finish in-flight requests: vLLM --shutdown-timeout), SIGKILL cannot be caught, SIGINT is Ctrl-C.
  • Shared memory (/dev/shm): NCCL and multi-process engines use it; in containers it must be enlarged (--shm-size or --ipc host).
  • Health endpoints: /health (alive), /v1/models (model loaded), /metrics (Prometheus text format).

HTTP, streaming and gRPC

  • HTTP/1.1 keeps a TCP connection alive for multiple requests; HTTP/2 multiplexes many streams over one connection (Envoy uses it to talk gRPC to the EPP).
  • Server-Sent Events (SSE): the response is text/event-stream; the server writes data: {...}\n\n chunks as tokens are produced and ends with data: [DONE]. This is how TTFT becomes visible to users.
  • gRPC = protobuf messages over HTTP/2. Envoy's ext_proc filter streams request/response headers and bodies to an external processor (the llm-d EPP) over gRPC and lets it mutate headers - e.g. set x-gateway-destination-endpoint to the chosen replica.

The OpenAI-compatible API

Both engines expose:

POST /v1/completions        {"model", "prompt", "max_tokens", "temperature", "stream"}
POST /v1/chat/completions   {"model", "messages":[{"role","content"}], "tools", "response_format", "stream"}
GET  /v1/models

The server applies the model's chat template (turns messages into one prompt string with special tokens), tokenizes, generates, detokenizes incrementally, and parses tool calls/reasoning if configured (--tool-call-parser, --reasoning-parser). Engine-specific extras ride in the same JSON (ignore_eos, kv_transfer_params, priority).

Timeouts and keep-alive

Every hop (client → CDN → gateway → Envoy → model server) has its own connection and idle timeouts. Long generations need long timeouts at every hop; mismatched keep-alive between a proxy and a server causes reset connections (the llm-d P/D guide sets VLLM_HTTP_TIMEOUT_KEEP_ALIVE=120 to exceed the sidecar's 90 s idle timeout).

lessons.title: Containers and Kubernetes for GPU serving
lessons.html:
Containers

A container is a process with its own filesystem image, namespaces (PID, network, mount) and cgroup limits (CPU, memory). For GPUs:

  • The NVIDIA Container Toolkit injects the driver libraries and device nodes: docker run --gpus '"device=0,1"' ... exposes GPUs 0 and 1 (seen inside as 0 and 1).
  • Images pin the whole user-space stack (CUDA runtime, PyTorch, vLLM, NCCL, NIXL/UCX), which is why the llm-d guides pin vllm/vllm-openai:v0.31.0.
  • --network host shares the host network stack (used in the no-k8s labs so everything talks over 127.0.0.1); --ipc host or --shm-size for shared memory.
  • Mount model weights from a cache volume instead of baking 60 GB into the image.

Kubernetes in one page

Object Purpose
Pod one or more containers scheduled together on a node, sharing network/IPC (e.g. vLLM + routing sidecar)
Deployment N identical pods, rolling updates, self-healing
Service stable virtual IP/DNS name load-balancing to pods selected by labels
ConfigMap / Secret config files and credentials (HF token)
PersistentVolumeClaim storage (model cache)
Node resources nvidia.com/gpu: 2 requests whole GPUs via the NVIDIA device plugin; DRA (resource.k8s.io/v1) is the newer claim-based model
Probes startup/readiness/liveness; readiness gates traffic until the model is loaded
HPA Horizontal Pod Autoscaler; scales replicas on metrics. KEDA feeds it external metrics (Prometheus) and can scale to zero
CRD + controller (operator) extend the API with new kinds, e.g. InferencePool, LeaderWorkerSet, DisaggregatedSet, InferenceObjective

Kubernetes is declarative: you apply desired state (YAML), controllers reconcile actual state toward it continuously.

Kubernetes objects used by llm-d

  • InferencePool (Gateway API Inference Extension): the set of model-server pods (by label selector) plus a reference to the EPP that picks among them.
  • LeaderWorkerSet (LWS): a replica made of a group of pods (leader + workers) that start, fail and roll out together - needed when one model replica spans several nodes (wide-EP, multi-node TP/PP).
  • DisaggregatedSet: prefill and decode LWS roles managed as one versioned unit (P/D, wide-EP).
  • Gateway API (Gateway, HTTPRoute): standard L7 ingress; llm-d can run in standalone mode (Envoy sidecar in the EPP pod) or gateway mode (Istio, agentgateway, GKE Gateway in front).

Packaging: Helm and Kustomize

  • Helm charts are templated packages with values files; llm-d's router ships as llm-d-router-standalone / llm-d-router-gateway charts, and guides layer values (base.values.yaml + <guide>.values.yaml).
  • Kustomize composes plain YAML with overlays and patches; llm-d model servers are overlays per accelerator / engine / provider (modelserver/gpu/vllm/base/).

lessons.title: Measuring LLM serving performance
lessons.html:
Latency metrics

request sent ──► first token ──► token 2 ──► ... ──► last token
|<--- TTFT --->|<- ITL ->|                         |
|<------------------------- E2E latency ---------->|
TPOT = (E2E − TTFT) / (output_tokens − 1)
  • TTFT (time to first token): queueing + prefill (+ network). What a chat user feels as "responsiveness".
  • ITL (inter-token latency): gap between consecutive streamed tokens; TPOT (time per output token) is its per-request average. Reading speed is ~5-10 tokens/s, so TPOT under ~50 ms feels instant for chat; agents and code generation want much lower.
  • E2E latency: total; dominates for non-streaming and agentic loops.

Report percentiles (p50, p90, p99), not just means: the p99 is what one in a hundred users sees, and in agentic workflows with many calls per task, tail latency compounds.

Throughput metrics

  • Output tokens/s (decode throughput) and total tokens/s (input + output).
  • Requests/s at a given latency SLO.
  • Goodput: requests/s that meet the SLO (e.g. TTFT < 1 s and TPOT < 50 ms). Throughput at unbounded latency is not useful.
  • Per-GPU or per-dollar normalization when comparing configs with different GPU counts (TP=8 vs 8 x TP=1).

Load generation

  • Closed loop (fixed concurrency, --max-concurrency): each client sends the next request when the previous finishes. Good for sweeping.
  • Open loop (fixed arrival rate, --request-rate, Poisson arrivals): closer to real traffic; queues grow without bound past capacity.
  • Workload shape matters more than anything: input/output lengths, prefix sharing, multi-turn reuse, burstiness. Benchmarks with random tokens get 0% prefix reuse; real chat traffic gets a lot.

Queueing intuition

Little's law: L = λ × W (items in system = arrival rate × time in system). At 20 req/s and 5 s average latency, 100 requests are in flight - that's the concurrency your servers must hold (and the KV cache must fit).

As utilization approaches 100%, waiting time grows sharply (an M/M/1 queue waits ~ρ/(1−ρ) service times; at 90% utilization that's 9x). That is why latency-sensitive services run with headroom, and why the router should queue centrally (flow control) instead of overfilling replica queues.

Benchmarking hygiene

  • Warm up (compile caches, CUDA graphs, first-request costs) before measuring.
  • Fix seeds, input/output lengths, and ignore_eos for comparable output lengths.
  • Change one variable at a time; record engine version, flags, GPU clocks.
  • Watch for client bottlenecks (a single Python client can't drive 10k tok/s without async I/O).
  • Check quality as well as speed when changing numerics.

lessons.title: vLLM track overview
lessons.html:
Twelve self-contained labs that take a base FP32 model and progressively apply the major serving optimizations available in vLLM, on an 8xB200 node - ending with a capstone that shows the full fp32-to-fully-optimized speedup.

Every lab launches a real vllm serve process, drives it with vllm bench serve, tears it down, and saves its results - no notebooks, no mocked timings. Each lab is runnable on its own, and run_all_labs.py (repo root) runs the whole track end to end and builds a consolidated report.

Prerequisites

  • 8x NVIDIA B200 (built/tuned against nvidia-smi reporting sm_100, 178GB/GPU - fewer GPUs work for every lab except Lab 10).
  • A working vLLM + CUDA environment. Known-good versions (see requirements.txt): vllm==0.26.0, torch==2.11.0, transformers==5.14.1.
  • HF_HOME pointed at fast, large local storage (labs assume /raid/llm_rl_cache/hf_home, override with the HF_HOME env var).
  • An HF_TOKEN with access to the gated meta-llama/* repos (accept the license on the model pages first).
  • Recommended on Blackwell: flashinfer-python (Lab 03 and Lab 08 skip variants gracefully if a backend or scheme is unavailable).

Quickstart

Run from the repository root:

# 1. Check your environment is ready
python scripts/check_env.py

# 2. Pre-fetch every model used by the labs (avoids downloads mid-benchmark)
export HF_TOKEN=hf_...
bash scripts/download_models.sh

# 3. Run everything
python run_all_labs.py

# ...or just smoke-test the whole suite quickly first
python run_all_labs.py --quick

# ...or run one lab standalone
python labs/lab04_prefix_caching/lab.py

Results land in results/: each lab writes results/<lab_name>/results.json, and every lab appends a section to results/SUMMARY.md, which becomes the one-page report of the whole fp32 -> optimized journey once you've run everything (Lab 11 adds the final rollup).

The labs

# Lab What it teaches GPUs
00 FP32 baseline Reference point every other lab compares against 1
01 Precision (fp32 -> fp16/bf16) The single biggest, lowest-risk win 1
02 Continuous batching + paged KV cache Naive HF static batching vs vLLM's scheduler 1
03 High-efficiency attention backends FlashInfer vs FlashAttention 4/2 vs Triton vs FlexAttention 1
04 Automatic prefix caching Reusing KV cache across requests with shared prefixes 1
05 Chunked prefill Keeping short requests responsive alongside long ones 1
06 CUDA graphs / compilation Eager vs -O0..-O2 and CUDA graph modes 1
07 Weight quantization (AWQ / GPTQ) INT4 checkpoints, memory vs throughput 1
08 FP8 / MX quantization (Blackwell-native) Online FP8 per-tensor/per-block, MXFP8, MXFP4, FP8 KV cache 1
09 Speculative decoding Draft model, EAGLE-3 and n-gram proposers; latency vs throughput 1-2
10 Tensor parallelism Scaling a 32B model across TP=1/2/4/8 up to 8
11 Capstone: full stack The complete fp32 -> optimized journey, both models up to 4

Each lab's own README has the concept explanation, the exact experiment, and what to look for in the results.

Why 12 labs instead of a single "PagedAttention" lab?

If you've read that PagedAttention is deprecated - you read correctly. vLLM deleted the original 2023 standalone PagedAttention kernel. The technique (paged, block-based KV cache management) didn't go away: it's built into every modern attention backend (FlashAttention, FlashInfer, Triton, FlexAttention). Lab 02 teaches the underlying concept; Lab 03 is a shootout between the backends that now carry it, including FlashAttention 4 (the default on SM100) and FlashInfer's TRT-LLM kernels.

How the suite is wired

  • common/config.py - every model ID, path, and default lives here. Override any of it via environment variables without touching code (e.g. LAB_MODEL_PRIMARY=some/other-model).
  • common/server.py - starts/stops a vllm serve subprocess, polls /health, and guarantees teardown (SIGTERM then SIGKILL, process-group wide) so GPU memory is actually free before the next lab starts.
  • common/bench.py - wraps vllm bench serve, parses its JSON result file, and can fire multiple benchmark workloads concurrently at the same server (used by Lab 05's mixed-traffic simulation).
  • common/report.py - console tables, speedup-vs-baseline columns, and the results/SUMMARY.md rollup.
  • common/hf_baseline.py - the deliberately naive HF transformers.generate() static-batching baseline used only by Lab 02, run in an isolated subprocess.
  • Every labs/<name>/lab.py exposes run(quick: bool, gpus: str | None) and a standalone CLI (--quick, --gpus), so run_all_labs.py and direct invocation share the exact same code path.

run_all_labs.py options

python run_all_labs.py --list              # show the lab order and exit
python run_all_labs.py --labs 0,1,3        # run a subset
python run_all_labs.py --quick             # shrink every workload for a fast smoke test
python run_all_labs.py --gpus 1            # override the default single GPU used by most labs

lessons.title: Lab 00: FP32 baseline
lessons.html:
Concept

Every other lab in this suite measures itself against this one. We serve the primary model (meta-llama/Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct) with vLLM at full FP32 precision - no quantization, no speculative decoding, nothing clever - and record:

  • Memory: weights alone are 8B params x 4 bytes = ~32GB.
  • Throughput: output tokens/sec and requests/sec under a fixed synthetic workload.
  • Latency: mean/P99 time-to-first-token (TTFT) and time-per-output-token (TPOT).

Every later lab (precision, quantization, caching, CUDA graphs, attention backends, ...) reruns the same workload shape and reports its speedup relative to these numbers.

Why FP32 at all?

Nobody serves LLMs in FP32 in production - it's 2x the memory and compute cost of BF16 for (in practice) no measurable quality benefit for inference. We start here on purpose: it's the "naive PyTorch default" starting point most people would reach for if they just called .float() on a checkpoint, and it makes the payoff of each subsequent optimization visible in the numbers instead of asserted in prose.

A preview of things to come

Watch the server log (results/logs/*fp32*.log) at startup. Because FP32 activations aren't supported by vLLM's fastest attention kernels (FlashInfer and FlashAttention both require FP16/BF16), vLLM will silently fall back to a slower attention backend (Triton or FlexAttention) just to run this lab at all. That's your first real hint about the relationship between precision and kernel choice - which is exactly what Lab 03 digs into.

What this lab does

  1. Launches vllm serve meta-llama/Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct --dtype float32 on one GPU.
  2. Runs vllm bench serve with a synthetic (random dataset) workload: ~512 input tokens / 128 output tokens per request, fired at unlimited request rate (--request-rate inf) so the server's own scheduler is the bottleneck.
  3. Saves the result to results/lab00_fp32_baseline/results.json for every later lab to load and compare against, and appends a section to results/SUMMARY.md.

Run it

python labs/lab00_fp32_baseline/lab.py            # full run
python labs/lab00_fp32_baseline/lab.py --quick     # fast smoke test
python labs/lab00_fp32_baseline/lab.py --gpus 1    # pin to a specific GPU

What to look for

  • Peak GPU memory usage (nvidia-smi snapshot printed before/after server start) - this is your reference point for "how much does precision / quantization actually save".
  • Note the achieved throughput is already using vLLM's continuous batching and paged KV cache - the "fp32" in this lab's name refers only to model precision, not to which serving techniques are enabled. Lab 02 is where we isolate the batching technique itself.

lessons.title: Lab 01: Precision reduction (FP32 -> FP16 / BF16)
lessons.html:
Concept

The single biggest, lowest-risk win in serving efficiency is simply not using FP32. Halving the bytes per parameter:

  • Halves weight memory (32GB -> 16GB for the 8B model), leaving far more headroom for KV cache (i.e. more concurrent requests).
  • Roughly doubles achievable throughput, since most modern GPU tensor cores (including B200's) are dramatically faster at FP16/BF16 matmuls than FP32.
  • Unlocks vLLM's fast attention backends entirely: FlashInfer and FlashAttention only support FP16/BF16 (see Lab 00's note and Lab 03).

BF16 vs FP16: same memory/throughput profile, different tradeoff. BF16 keeps FP32's 8-bit exponent (same dynamic range, less mantissa precision) so it rarely needs loss scaling and is what most modern LLMs are trained/released in. FP16 has more mantissa bits (more precision) but a much smaller dynamic range, which can matter for numerical stability. On Blackwell both run at the same tensor-core throughput, so BF16 is the practical default; FP16 is included here mainly so you can see that for yourself.

What this lab does

Serves meta-llama/Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct with --dtype float16 and --dtype bfloat16 (same GPU, same synthetic workload as Lab 00), then prints a combined table alongside Lab 00's saved FP32 numbers with speedup ratios.

Run it

python labs/lab01_precision_bf16_fp16/lab.py
python labs/lab01_precision_bf16_fp16/lab.py --quick

Run Lab 00 first (or at least once) so this lab has a baseline row to compare against; if it hasn't been run yet, this lab still works, it just skips the comparison row.

What to look for

  • Memory drop after server start (nvidia-smi snapshot) - should be roughly half of Lab 00's.
  • output_throughput (tokens/sec) - typically ~1.5-2x FP32 on B200.
  • Which attention backend vLLM selects now that FP16/BF16 is available (check the server log) - this is worth comparing to Lab 00's log.

lessons.title: Lab 02: Continuous batching + paged KV cache
lessons.html:
Concept

This is the idea that made vLLM famous, so it's worth being precise about what it actually is (a scheduling + memory-management technique) versus what it's called in the code today (see the callout below).

Static batching (the naive approach): collect a batch of N requests, run model.generate() until every sequence in the batch is done, return all N results, repeat. The problem: if one sequence in the batch needs 500 tokens and the rest need 20, the whole batch - and the GPU - is stuck waiting on that one straggler. Short requests that finished early still occupy a batch slot and its KV cache reservation until the whole batch retires.

Continuous batching: at every scheduler step, evict sequences that just finished and admit new sequences waiting in the queue, so the batch composition changes every step instead of being fixed for its whole lifetime. Throughput is limited by GPU compute, not by the slowest member of an arbitrarily-drawn batch.

Paged KV cache: the memory technique that makes continuous batching practical. Instead of reserving one contiguous max_seq_len-sized KV buffer per sequence (mostly wasted for short sequences), the cache is divided into fixed-size blocks allocated on demand, like OS virtual memory pages. This is what lets sequences of wildly different lengths share GPU memory efficiently and lets the scheduler admit/evict sequences cheaply.

A note on the name "PagedAttention"

You may have heard that PagedAttention is "deprecated" - this is true at the implementation level and misleading at the concept level. vLLM v0.25.0 (July 2026) deleted the original, standalone 2023 PagedAttention CUDA kernel. It didn't disappear because the idea failed; it disappeared because the technique - block-based paged KV memory - is now built directly into every modern attention backend (FlashInfer, FlashAttention, Triton, FlexAttention) under vLLM's Model Runner V2, which has been the default execution path for a while. There's no longer a separate "paged attention toggle"; every backend paged the KV cache. Lab 03 is dedicated to comparing those backends against each other.

What this lab does

  1. Runs a deliberately naive HF Transformers static-batch baseline (common/hf_baseline.py, launched as its own subprocess) against a set of prompts with intentionally bimodal output lengths (half one-sentence answers, half multi-paragraph essays) - this bimodality is what makes the "batch straggler" effect visible.
  2. Serves the same model with vLLM and fires the same number of requests at once via vllm bench serve --max-concurrency, in two configurations:
    • --max-num-seqs 8: capped at the same concurrency as the HF batch size, isolating the effect of continuous batching itself (same concurrency budget, no static-batch bubble).
    • default --max-num-seqs: letting vLLM use its normal scheduling headroom.

Run it

python labs/lab02_continuous_batching_paged_kv_cache/lab.py
python labs/lab02_continuous_batching_paged_kv_cache/lab.py --quick

What to look for

  • hf_naive_static_batch vs vllm_max_num_seqs_8: same effective concurrency limit, but vLLM should still substantially outperform HF's generate() loop because it isn't blocked by the slowest sequence in each fixed batch.
  • vllm_max_num_seqs_8 vs vllm_default: shows the throughput you leave on the table by artificially constraining concurrency.

lessons.title: Lab 03: High-efficiency attention backends
lessons.html:
Concept

As covered in Lab 02: the original standalone PagedAttention kernel is gone (removed in vLLM v0.25.0, July 2026). What's left to tune is which attention backend vLLM uses, since paged KV-cache management now lives inside each backend's own kernels. On NVIDIA Blackwell (B200, SM100), the backends you can pick for a standard GQA decoder like Llama-3.1-8B are:

Backend Notes
FLASH_ATTN FlashAttention. Version is selectable with --attention-config.flash_attn_version=2/3/4; FA4 is the default on SM100+, FA3 on Hopper, FA2 elsewhere. Automatic selection tries FlashAttention first.
FLASHINFER FlashInfer. On SM100 it uses the trtllm-gen decode kernels (with attention-sink support and native FP8 KV); disable with --attention-config.use_trtllm_attention=0. Part of vLLM's Blackwell fallback order (TRT-LLM ragged → FlashInfer → ...).
TRITON_ATTN Pure-Triton attention kernel. Slower than the two above but has no extra native-kernel dependency and supports dtypes/shapes the others don't (e.g. FP32, used unavoidably in Lab 00).
FLEX_ATTENTION PyTorch's flex_attention, compiled via torch.compile. Flexible (custom masks/score-mods) but generally the slowest for plain causal attention.

Multimodal models get composite backends such as TRITON_FLASHINFER (Triton for bidirectional image-prefix attention, FlashInfer for causal text), picked automatically - not relevant for this text-only lab, but worth knowing.

Selecting a backend (current vLLM)

The old VLLM_ATTENTION_BACKEND environment variable has been replaced by a CLI flag / structured config (the two forms are mutually exclusive):

vllm serve <model> --attention-backend FLASHINFER
vllm serve <model> --attention-config '{"backend": "FLASH_ATTN", "flash_attn_version": 2}'
vllm serve <model> -ac.backend TRITON_ATTN

When you pick a backend explicitly, vLLM validates it against the model (dtype, head size, compute capability) and errors out with the reason if it is incompatible; this lab reports that as "skipped". With no flag, vLLM walks a priority list and takes the first compatible backend.

Why prefill vs decode matters

Attention backends don't all have the same strengths. A backend can be excellent at prefill (processing a long prompt's tokens in parallel, compute-bound) and mediocre at decode (one new token at a time per sequence, memory-bandwidth/launch-overhead-bound), or vice versa. This lab runs two workload profiles against every backend:

  • Prefill-heavy: long input (~4000 tokens), short output (~32 tokens), many concurrent requests - stresses the prefill path.
  • Decode-heavy: short input (~128 tokens), long output (~512 tokens), low concurrency (4) - stresses the per-token decode path.

What this lab does

For each variant (FlashInfer, FlashAttention 4, FlashAttention 2, Triton, FlexAttention): launch vllm serve with the backend flag, run the prefill-heavy and decode-heavy benchmarks, tear down, move on. Any variant that fails to start is reported as skipped rather than failing the lab.

Run it

python labs/lab03_attention_backends/lab.py
python labs/lab03_attention_backends/lab.py --quick

What to look for

  • FA4 vs FA2 on the prefill-heavy run: FA4 is written for Blackwell's tensor memory and async TMA pipeline, so the gap should be largest on long prompts.
  • Decode-heavy mean_tpot_ms (time per output token) is usually where the backends differentiate most sharply.
  • Check results/logs/lab03_<backend>_*.log for the line where vLLM reports the backend it actually selected.

lessons.title: Lab 04: Automatic prefix caching (APC)
lessons.html:
Concept

Many real workloads send requests that share a long common prefix: a system prompt, a few-shot example block, a RAG context chunk reused across several questions, or successive turns of the same chat. Without prefix caching, vLLM re-runs the full prefill computation for that shared prefix on every single request. With automatic prefix caching, the paged KV blocks for a prefix are kept around (as long as memory allows) and reused by any later request whose tokens start with the same prefix - turning an O(prefix length) prefill into an O(1) cache lookup for every request after the first.

The benefit shows up almost entirely as reduced time-to-first-token (TTFT): less new computation before the response begins, not more output tokens/sec.

What this lab does

Uses vllm bench serve's built-in random dataset with --random-prefix-len 1500 - every synthetic request shares an identical 1500-token random prefix, plus its own random 200-token suffix, and expects a 100-token completion. Runs this workload once with --no-enable-prefix-caching and once with prefix caching enabled (vLLM's current default), same server otherwise.

Within a single run, only the first request pays the full 1500-token prefill; every request after it should hit the cache when caching is enabled. With ~80 requests sharing the prefix, that dominates the mean/P99 TTFT - which is exactly what you should see move between the two variants.

Run it

python labs/lab04_prefix_caching/lab.py
python labs/lab04_prefix_caching/lab.py --quick

What to look for

  • mean_ttft_ms and p99_ttft_ms: should drop substantially with prefix caching on, since ~79/80 requests skip re-prefilling the shared 1500 tokens.
  • output_throughput: caching frees up GPU compute that was being spent on redundant prefill, so overall throughput should also improve, not just latency.

lessons.title: Lab 05: Chunked prefill
lessons.html:
Concept

Prefill (processing a prompt's tokens for the first time) and decode (generating one new token per sequence) have very different compute profiles: prefill is compute-bound and scales with prompt length, decode is comparatively cheap but latency-sensitive. Without chunked prefill, a single very long prompt's prefill can occupy an entire scheduler step, during which no other sequence's decode step runs - so a handful of short, latency-sensitive requests can get stuck behind one long document being ingested.

Chunked prefill splits a long prompt's prefill into smaller chunks and interleaves them with other sequences' decode steps across multiple scheduler iterations, instead of processing the whole prompt in one go. Short requests keep making progress every step instead of queueing behind a long one.

What this lab does

Simulates realistic mixed traffic by firing two concurrent workloads at the same running server (via common/bench.run_concurrent):

  • A trickle of long documents: ~6000-token prompts, low request rate.
  • A stream of short, latency-sensitive requests: ~100-token prompts, higher request rate.

Runs this mixed workload twice: once with --no-enable-chunked-prefill, once with chunked prefill enabled (vLLM's current default). The metric that matters is the short-request stream's TTFT while the long requests are in flight.

Run it

python labs/lab05_chunked_prefill/lab.py
python labs/lab05_chunked_prefill/lab.py --quick

What to look for

  • chunked_prefill_off_short vs chunked_prefill_on_short: look at p99_ttft_ms specifically - the tail latency of short requests is where the "blocked behind a long prefill" effect shows up most clearly.
  • The _long rows are there for context (throughput on the long-document stream itself), not the main point of the lab.

lessons.title: Lab 06: CUDA graphs / compilation
lessons.html:
Concept

Every forward pass through a model involves launching hundreds of small CUDA kernels. At small batch sizes (the common case for low-latency, low-concurrency decode), the CPU-side overhead of launching those kernels can rival or exceed the GPU time actually spent computing them.

CUDA graphs capture a fixed sequence of kernel launches once and replay the whole graph with a single call, eliminating per-kernel launch overhead. vLLM also runs torch.compile over the model to fuse ops (e.g. RMSNorm + quant, SiLU-mul + quant, allreduce + RMSNorm) before graph capture.

Optimization levels (current vLLM)

Flag What you get
--enforce-eager No compilation and no CUDA graphs. Fastest startup, slowest decode.
-O0 No optimizations.
-O1 Fast compilation and simple fusions, PIECEWISE CUDA graphs.
-O2 (default) More compile ranges and fusions, FULL_AND_PIECEWISE CUDA graphs.
-O3 Aggressive; currently equal to -O2.

The CUDA graph mode is the single knob in --compilation-config '{"cudagraph_mode": "..."}', one of NONE, PIECEWISE, FULL, FULL_DECODE_ONLY, FULL_AND_PIECEWISE:

  • PIECEWISE graphs everything except attention (attention runs eagerly between graph pieces) - works with every attention backend.
  • FULL graphs the whole forward pass including attention - needs the attention backend to support graph capture.
  • FULL_AND_PIECEWISE uses full graphs for uniform decode batches and piecewise graphs for mixed prefill+decode batches (the default).
  • FULL_DECODE_ONLY uses full graphs for decode, eager for mixed batches - less memory spent on captured graphs, useful with P/D disaggregation.

(The old {"level": 3} compilation-config key has been replaced by -O<n> / "mode".)

What this lab does

Runs five variants (--enforce-eager, -O0, -O1, -O2, and -O2 with FULL_DECODE_ONLY) at two concurrency levels:

  • Low concurrency (max-concurrency=1): isolates per-token decode latency, where CUDA graphs matter most.
  • High concurrency (max-concurrency=64): the workload becomes more compute-bound, so the relative benefit of CUDA graphs should shrink.

Run it

python labs/lab06_cuda_graphs_compilation/lab.py
python labs/lab06_cuda_graphs_compilation/lab.py --quick

What to look for

  • eager_low vs O2_default_low: mean_tpot_ms should be noticeably higher (worse) under --enforce-eager.
  • O1_piecewise vs O2_default: the extra gain from capturing attention inside full graphs.
  • The _high runs: the gaps shrink as each step does more GPU work.
  • Startup time in results/logs/lab06_*.log: compilation and graph capture add tens of seconds (cached under ~/.cache/vllm/torch_compile_cache on later runs) - the tradeoff for faster steady-state decode.

lessons.title: Lab 07: Weight-only quantization (AWQ / GPTQ)
lessons.html:
Concept

BF16 halved FP32's memory footprint; weight-only quantization goes further by storing weights in 4 bits instead of 16, while keeping activations in a higher-precision compute dtype. Two popular post-training quantization methods:

  • AWQ (Activation-aware Weight Quantization): protects the small fraction of "salient" weight channels most sensitive to quantization error (identified from activation statistics) by keeping them at higher effective precision, quantizing the rest to INT4.
  • GPTQ: a one-shot weight quantization method that greedily minimizes layer-wise reconstruction error using second-order (Hessian) information, quantizing to INT4 (or INT8) with typically small accuracy loss.

Both need a calibration/quantization pass done ahead of time against a calibration dataset - this lab uses ready-made community checkpoints rather than re-deriving them, since that's how most teams actually consume quantized models. The interesting comparison for a serving lab is memory and throughput, not the quantization algorithm's internals.

What this lab does

Serves three checkpoints of the same base model back to back:

  1. BF16 (reuses Lab 01's saved result if available, otherwise reruns it).
  2. hugging-quants/Meta-Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct-AWQ-INT4
  3. hugging-quants/Meta-Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct-GPTQ-INT4

vLLM auto-detects the quantization method from each checkpoint's config, so no explicit --quantization flag is needed.

Run it

python labs/lab07_weight_quantization_awq_gptq/lab.py
python labs/lab07_weight_quantization_awq_gptq/lab.py --quick

What to look for

  • GPU memory snapshot right after each server starts: weights should drop from ~16GB (bf16) to roughly 5-6GB (INT4) for the 8B model.
  • output_throughput: INT4 quantization reduces memory-bandwidth pressure (fewer bytes moved per weight read), which often increases throughput even though there's dequantization overhead - especially at memory-bandwidth-bound batch sizes.
  • This lab does not measure output quality/accuracy - that requires a task benchmark (e.g. lm-eval-harness), which is out of scope here. Quantization always trades some accuracy for memory/speed; AWQ and GPTQ are both designed to minimize that loss, not eliminate it.

lessons.title: Lab 08: FP8 quantization (Blackwell-native)
lessons.html:
Concept

B200 (Blackwell, SM100) has native FP8 tensor cores - unlike AWQ/GPTQ INT4 (Lab 07), FP8 quantization here needs no pre-quantized checkpoint or calibration step: vLLM can quantize a BF16 checkpoint to FP8 dynamically at load time with --quantization fp8 (per-tensor/per-channel dynamic scales computed on the fly). This gets you roughly half the weight memory of BF16 with much less accuracy risk than INT4, backed by hardware that runs FP8 matmuls at full speed.

FP8 also applies to the KV cache independently of weight precision (--kv-cache-dtype fp8_e4m3): halving KV cache bytes-per-token means either more concurrent sequences at the same memory budget, or a larger usable context length.

This connects directly to Lab 03: on Blackwell, vLLM's default attention backend (FlashInfer) ships a decode-optimized trtllm-gen kernel path with native FP8 (and NVFP4) support - so FP8 here isn't just "smaller", it's running through hardware-accelerated kernels rather than a generic quantize/dequantize fallback.

Online quantization schemes (current vLLM)

Scheme Weights Activations Notes
fp8_per_tensor FP8 E4M3, one FP32 scale per tensor FP8, per-tensor (per-token on some GPUs) Simplest; what --quantization fp8 used to mean.
fp8_per_block FP8, one scale per 128x128 block FP8, one scale per 1x128 block DeepSeek-style; more robust to outliers.
mxfp8 FP8 E4M3 + E8M0 scale per 1x32 block same OCP microscaling; native w8a8 on SM100+.
mxfp4 FP4 E2M1 + E8M0 scale per 1x32 block backend-dependent (FP4 or BF16) Quarter of BF16 weight memory; accuracy cost is higher.

What this lab does

Serves the primary model as:

  1. BF16 (reused from Lab 01 if available).
  2. fp8_per_tensor, fp8_per_block, mxfp8, mxfp4 (quantized weights, BF16 KV cache).
  3. fp8_per_tensor + --kv-cache-dtype fp8_e4m3 (FP8 weights and KV cache).

Any scheme your installed vLLM doesn't recognise is reported as skipped.

Run it

python labs/lab08_fp8_quantization/lab.py
python labs/lab08_fp8_quantization/lab.py --quick

What to look for

  • GPU memory after server start: FP8 weights should be roughly half of BF16's; adding FP8 KV cache reduces it further, most visibly at higher concurrency where KV cache (not weights) dominates memory.
  • output_throughput: FP8 matmuls on B200 should outperform BF16, unlike a non-native-FP8 GPU where the dequantization overhead could eat the memory savings.
  • Check the server log for which attention backend was selected - if FlashInfer is available, FP8 attention should be running through the trtllm-gen path discussed in Lab 03.

lessons.title: Lab 09: Speculative decoding
lessons.html:
Concept

Normal decoding generates exactly one token per forward pass per sequence. Speculative decoding has a cheap "proposer" guess several tokens ahead, then verifies all of them in a single forward pass of the real (target) model - if the target model agrees with a guessed token, you get it for free; the first disagreement is the fallback point. Because verification is one batched forward pass regardless of how many tokens were proposed, you can get multiple tokens per target-model step when the proposer guesses well, at zero cost in output distribution (the outputs are mathematically identical to standard decoding, provided the acceptance rule is used correctly).

Three proposer strategies compared here, all configured through --speculative-config '{"method": ..., ...}':

  • Draft-model speculation ("method": "draft_model"): a small, fast model (Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct) proposes tokens for the target model (Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct) to verify. Works well when the draft model's outputs correlate well with the target's.
  • EAGLE-3 ("method": "eagle3"): instead of a separate LM, a tiny one-layer head (RedHatAI/Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct-speculator.eagle3) reads the target model's own hidden states (from low, middle and high layers) and predicts the next few tokens. Much cheaper than a draft LM and usually the best acceptance rate - this is what production deployments use today.
  • N-gram / prompt-lookup speculation: no draft model at all - propose tokens by looking for repeated n-grams earlier in the prompt/generation so far. Free to run, and surprisingly effective for tasks with a lot of copying/repetition (code editing, summarization, structured extraction).

Why concurrency matters here

Speculative decoding helps most when the target model is not already compute-saturated - i.e. low concurrency, latency-sensitive serving. At high concurrency, the GPU is already busy doing useful work for many sequences, so the extra verification forward passes (and a rejected guess is pure waste) can make speculative decoding neutral or even a net throughput loss. This lab measures both regimes deliberately.

What this lab does

Four variants (no speculation baseline, draft-model, EAGLE-3, n-gram), each benchmarked at:

  • Low concurrency (max-concurrency=2): the latency-sensitive regime where speculative decoding should win.
  • High concurrency (max-concurrency=64): the throughput regime where the benefit should shrink or reverse.

Run it

python labs/lab09_speculative_decoding/lab.py
python labs/lab09_speculative_decoding/lab.py --quick

What to look for

  • no_spec_low vs draft_model_spec_low / ngram_spec_low: mean_tpot_ms should drop (fewer wall-clock ms per output token) when speculation is accepted often.
  • The same comparison at _high: the gap should be much smaller, or even favor no_spec.
  • vLLM logs speculative acceptance metrics (mean acceptance length, per-position acceptance rate) in the server log and on /metrics (vllm:spec_decode_*) - compare EAGLE-3 vs the draft model there.
  • Beyond this lab, upstream also has MTP heads (for models trained with multi-token prediction such as DeepSeek-V3), suffix decoding, and dynamic speculation (num_speculative_tokens_per_batch_size) that shrinks k as concurrency grows.
  • ngram_spec works with zero extra model-loading cost - worth comparing its win rate against the draft-model approach on this specific synthetic (random-token) workload, which has little natural repetition, so n-gram speculation is a harder case here than on a real repetitive task.

lessons.title: Lab 10: Tensor parallelism
lessons.html:
Concept

Every other lab uses the 8B primary model, which comfortably fits on one B200. This lab switches to Qwen/Qwen2.5-32B-Instruct (ungated, ~64GB in BF16) specifically to make tensor parallelism (TP) worth doing.

Tensor parallelism shards individual weight matrices (attention projections, MLP layers) across multiple GPUs, so each GPU holds and computes on only 1/TP of every layer. Every layer requires an all-reduce (or similar collective) across the TP group to combine partial results, so TP trades GPU memory/compute headroom for inter-GPU communication - which is exactly why it matters that B200s in this node are connected over fast NVLink rather than PCIe alone.

What this lab does

  1. Serves Qwen2.5-32B-Instruct in BF16 at --tensor-parallel-size 1, 2, 4, and 8 (using the first N GPUs from your pool for each), running the same benchmark workload at each size and recording throughput/latency.
  2. Bonus (full run only, skipped under --quick): a memory-pressure check - serving the same 32B model at FP32 with TP=1. At FP32, weights alone are 32B x 4 bytes = ~128GB, leaving only ~50GB of a B200's 179GB for the framework, activations, and KV cache. This either succeeds with a very small usable KV cache (few concurrent requests / short context) or fails outright with an out-of-memory error - both outcomes are informative, and this variant is wrapped so a failure here doesn't fail the whole lab.

Run it

python labs/lab10_tensor_parallelism/lab.py
python labs/lab10_tensor_parallelism/lab.py --quick        # TP=1,2 only, skips the fp32 bonus
python labs/lab10_tensor_parallelism/lab.py --gpus 0,1,2,3,4,5,6,7   # explicit GPU pool

What to look for

  • Throughput scaling from TP=1 -> 2 -> 4 -> 8: expect solid gains from 1->2 and 1->4, with diminishing returns by TP=8 as all-reduce communication overhead starts to compete with the compute time saved per GPU.
  • mean_tpot_ms at each TP size: more GPUs means each one does less compute per step, but pays a fixed communication cost every layer - latency doesn't necessarily improve as much as raw throughput does.
  • Whether the FP32/TP=1 bonus variant succeeded or OOM'd, and if it succeeded, how small the achievable KV cache / concurrency was compared to the BF16 variants - this is the "why you'd reach for TP or quantization" moment for large models.

lessons.title: Lab 11: Capstone - the full optimization stack
lessons.html:
Concept

This lab doesn't introduce a new technique - it pulls together everything from Labs 00-10 into the "fp32 -> fully optimized" journey, on both models.

One thing worth internalizing by this point: most of the optimizations in this suite are already the default in modern vLLM. Continuous batching, paged KV cache, prefix caching, chunked prefill, and CUDA graphs are all on unless you explicitly disable them. The knobs you actually have to reach for in practice are the ones this capstone varies: precision / quantization, and (for models too large for one GPU) tensor parallelism. Everything else, vLLM is already doing for you.

What this lab does

8B journey (reuses saved results from earlier labs where available, reruns anything missing):

  1. fp32 (Lab 00)
  2. bfloat16 (Lab 01)
  3. fp8_weights_and_kv (Lab 08) - the "fully optimized single-GPU" config

32B journey (Qwen2.5-32B-Instruct, TP=4):

  1. tp4_bf16 (Lab 10)
  2. tp4_fp8 - adds FP8 weight quantization on top of TP=4

Both journeys get a cumulative speedup column relative to their first entry, and everything is appended to results/SUMMARY.md as the final section - the one-page summary of the whole suite.

Run it

python labs/lab11_capstone_full_stack/lab.py
python labs/lab11_capstone_full_stack/lab.py --quick

Running the full suite first (python run_all_labs.py) means this lab reuses everyone else's saved numbers instead of re-running servers; run standalone and it will backfill whatever's missing itself.

What to look for

  • The total speedup from fp32 to fp8_weights_and_kv on the 8B model - this is the number that answers the original question ("how much can I actually speed up serving a base fp32 model with vLLM on B200?").
  • Whether tp4_fp8 beats tp4_bf16 by roughly the same margin FP8 gave the 8B model - quantization and parallelism are largely orthogonal levers and should compose.
  • Check results/SUMMARY.md after this lab runs: it now contains every lab's table plus this final rollup, in one file.

The knobs you actually have to reach for in practice are the ones this capstone varies: precision / quantization, and (for models too large for one GPU) tensor parallelism. Everything else, vLLM is already doing for you.

lessons.title: SGLang track overview
lessons.html:
A hands-on curriculum for taking a base FP32-precision LLM to an efficiently served, production-tuned deployment on SGLang, built for a single 8xNVIDIA B200 node.

Each lab is self-contained: it has its own README.md (concept explanation + what to expect), its own run_lab.sh (launches SGLang server(s), runs benchmarks, records results, cleans up after itself), and can be run independently in any order after lab00_setup. A top-level run_all_labs.sh runs the whole curriculum end to end.

The curriculum

# Lab What it teaches
00 lab00_setup Isolated SGLang install, model downloads, smoke test
01 lab01_fp32_baseline Naive HF loop vs SGLang server, the "before" numbers
02 lab02_precision FP32 vs BF16 vs FP16
03 lab03_quantization FP8 (online) vs AWQ/GPTQ INT4 (pre-quantized)
04 lab04_tensor_parallelism TP scaling (1/2/4/8 GPUs), communication overhead
05 lab05_radix_attention RadixAttention automatic prefix caching
06 lab06_scheduling_batching Overlap scheduler, chunked prefill, queue policy
07 lab07_cuda_graph_torch_compile CUDA graphs & torch.compile
08 lab08_speculative_decoding N-gram speculative decoding (no draft model needed)
09 lab09_structured_output Grammar-guided JSON Schema decoding
10 lab10_moe_expert_parallel MoE: Expert Parallelism & DP Attention
11 lab11_capstone Stack the wins, measure total speedup, final charts
12 lab12_attention_backends FA4 vs FlashInfer vs TRT-LLM MHA vs Triton on Blackwell
13 lab13_hierarchical_cache HiCache: GPU -> CPU tiered KV cache behind RadixAttention

Every lab writes its raw results to results/<lab_name>/ and appends a row per configuration to results/summary.csv, so lab11_capstone (and you) can compare across the whole curriculum at the end.

Prerequisites

  • The 8xB200 node you described (nvidia-smi showing 8x B200, 183GB each, CUDA 13.0 driver).
  • conda on PATH (lab00 creates a dedicated sglang-labs environment; it intentionally does not touch whatever env your existing vLLM/DeepSpeed/etc. stack lives in).
  • Internet access to Hugging Face Hub and PyPI (or a pre-warmed $HF_HOME cache and pip mirror, if this node is air-gapped, in which case see lab00_setup/README.md for the Docker-based alternative).
  • ~150GB free disk for model weights (you have 27TB free on /raid -- trivial) and a few more GB for the sglang-labs conda environment.

Quick start

cd vllm_labs/sglang
./run_all_labs.sh              # runs lab00 through lab13, in order (a few hours total)

Or work through it incrementally, reading each README as you go:

cd vllm_labs/sglang/lab00_setup && ./run_lab.sh   # do this first, always
cd ../lab01_fp32_baseline && ./run_lab.sh
cd ../lab02_precision && ./run_lab.sh
# ...etc, or:
cd .. && ./run_all_labs.sh --from lab02

Useful run_all_labs.sh flags:

./run_all_labs.sh --list                  # show the lab order
./run_all_labs.sh --only lab03,lab08      # run just these labs
./run_all_labs.sh --skip lab04,lab10      # skip the multi/8-GPU-heavy labs
./run_all_labs.sh --from lab05            # resume from a specific lab
./run_all_labs.sh --dry-run               # print the plan without running anything

Configuration

Every knob lives in common/env.sh with sensible defaults, and can be overridden via environment variables without editing any file, e.g.:

SMALL_MODEL=Qwen/Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct BENCH_MAX_CONCURRENCY=128 ./run_all_labs.sh --only lab02

Key variables: SMALL_MODEL, MID_MODEL, MOE_MODEL (the three checkpoints used across the curriculum -- see lab00_setup/README.md for why these were chosen), HF_HOME, SGLANG_CONDA_ENV, BENCH_NUM_PROMPTS / BENCH_MAX_CONCURRENCY / BENCH_RANDOM_INPUT_LEN / BENCH_RANDOM_OUTPUT_LEN (default benchmark load shape).

How each lab is structured

labNN_topic/
  README.md      <- read this first: background, what the lab measures, expected results
  run_lab.sh      <- launches server(s), runs sglang.bench_serving, records + tears down
  *.py            <- any custom client/benchmark scripts specific to that lab

Shared infrastructure lives in common/:

  • env.sh -- central configuration (models, ports, paths, benchmark defaults).
  • lib.sh -- bash helpers: start/stop an SGLang server with health-check polling, GPU memory helpers, benchmark runner, result recording.
  • bench_lib.py -- parses sglang.bench_serving JSON output into results/summary.csv.
  • plot_results.py -- renders results/summary.csv into comparison bar charts (used by lab11_capstone).

Why this structure

  • Self-contained labs: every lab can be understood and re-run on its own -- read one README.md, run one run_lab.sh. Nothing requires reverse-engineering a shared framework to understand what a single lab is doing.
  • One variable at a time: each lab changes exactly one axis (precision, quantization, parallelism, caching, scheduling, speculative decoding, structured output, MoE parallelism) while holding everything else fixed, so the throughput/latency numbers you see are attributable to that one change.
  • Honest baselines: lab01 measures a genuinely naive serving path (plain transformers.generate() in a loop) so later speedup numbers mean something, instead of comparing two already-optimized configurations against each other.
  • Real SGLang docs, real flags: every server flag used across these labs was verified against SGLang's current server_arguments and feature docs (linked from each lab's README) rather than guessed from memory -- SGLang's CLI surface changes fast across releases, so if a flag has been renamed by the time you run this, python -m sglang.launch_server --help is always the ground truth.

Troubleshooting

  • Server fails to start on Blackwell (sgl_kernel / SM100 errors): see the "Blackwell troubleshooting" section in lab00_setup/README.md.
  • OOM during a lab: lower BENCH_MAX_CONCURRENCY, or add --mem-fraction-static 0.7 (or lower) to that lab's start_sglang_server call in its run_lab.sh.
  • A lab hangs waiting for the server to become healthy: check results/<lab>/server_*.log for the actual error; big models can legitimately take several minutes to load + capture CUDA graphs, so SERVER_STARTUP_TIMEOUT in common/env.sh is generous (1200s) by default, but you can raise it further if needed.
  • Leftover GPU memory between runs: common/lib.sh's stop_sglang_server and run_all_labs.sh's between-lab cleanup both pkill any stray sglang.launch_server processes and wait for nvidia-smi to report freed memory, but if you Ctrl-C mid-lab you may need to do this by hand: pkill -9 -f sglang.launch_server.

lessons.title: Lab 00 - Environment Setup
lessons.html:
Goal: get a clean, isolated SGLang install working on your 8xB200 node, and pre-download every model the rest of the curriculum needs.

Why a separate conda env?

Your node already has a conda env with torch 2.11.0+cu130, vllm 0.26.0, deepspeed, etc. SGLang ships its own tight pins on torch, flashinfer, and sgl-kernel (its custom CUDA kernel package, which must match your CUDA toolkit and GPU architecture -- B200 is sm_100, Blackwell). Installing SGLang into an env that already has vLLM's own flash-attn / kernel stack is one of the most common sources of "works in one process, segfaults in another" bugs. We create a new env, sglang-labs, and leave your existing env untouched.

What this lab does

  1. install_sglang.sh - creates the sglang-labs conda env (Python 3.11) and installs sglang[all] targeting the CUDA 13.0 build that matches your driver (nvidia-smi reported CUDA Version: 13.0). It also (re)installs flashinfer-python, which provides the fused attention kernels SGLang uses by default on sm75+ GPUs including B200.
  2. download_models.sh - pre-fetches every checkpoint used later:
    • Qwen/Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct - the small model used in labs 00-03, 05-09
    • Qwen/Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct-AWQ and -GPTQ-Int4 - pre-quantized variants for lab03
    • Qwen/Qwen2.5-32B-Instruct - the mid-size model used for TP scaling in lab04
    • Qwen/Qwen3-30B-A3B - a Mixture-of-Experts model used in lab10 All models are ungated (no HF token needed) and land in $HF_HOME (defaults to /raid/llm_rl_cache/hf_home, matching your existing cache location, ~150GB total).
  3. verify_install.sh - boots the small model on 1 GPU, sends one chat completion request, and shuts the server down again.

Run it

cd vllm_labs/sglang/lab00_setup
./run_lab.sh

This takes ~10-30 minutes depending on network speed (mostly model downloads). Re-running is safe; each step skips work that's already done.

Blackwell (B200 / sm_100) troubleshooting

SGLang's custom kernel package, sgl-kernel, ships architecture-specific wheels. If verify_install.sh fails at server startup with an error like:

RuntimeError: ... expected SM100 variant ... sgl_kernel ...

it means pip resolved a sgl-kernel build that doesn't include Blackwell (sm_100) kernels. Fix it by force-reinstalling the CUDA-13-tagged wheel directly from the SGLang wheel index (adjust the version to whatever python -c "import sglang; print(sglang.__version__)" reports):

conda activate sglang-labs
pip uninstall -y sgl-kernel
pip install "sgl-kernel==<version>+cu130" \
  --extra-index-url https://docs.sglang.ai/whl/cu130/

If pip/uv installation continues to be painful, the SGLang team's officially supported path for CUDA 13 hosts is the prebuilt Docker image, which bundles matching torch/flashinfer/sgl-kernel versions:

docker run --gpus all --shm-size 32g --ipc=host \
  -p 30000:30000 \
  -v /raid/llm_rl_cache/hf_home:/root/.cache/huggingface \
  lmsysorg/sglang:latest-cu130-runtime \
  python3 -m sglang.launch_server --model-path Qwen/Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct --host 0.0.0.0 --port 30000

If you go the Docker route, every other lab's run_lab.sh still works - just replace the start_sglang_server call in common/lib.sh with the equivalent docker run ... invocation, or run docker exec into a long-lived container that has the sglang-labs conda env's equivalent packages installed.

What you should understand after this lab

  • Why SGLang benefits from an isolated environment on multi-framework research nodes.
  • The two SGLang benchmarking entry points you'll use throughout the curriculum: python -m sglang.launch_server (the OpenAI-compatible server) and python -m sglang.bench_serving (the async load generator).
  • Where model weights and results live ($HF_HOME, results/).

lessons.title: Lab 01 - The Naive FP32 Baseline
lessons.html:
Goal: establish honest "before" numbers for the rest of the curriculum. Every subsequent lab reports its speedup relative to what you measure here.

Background

The task says "take a base FP32 precision model." In practice almost no model is published in true FP32 anymore (checkpoints on the Hub are usually BF16), so we treat FP32 as our deliberately-naive starting point: we force the model to load and run its weights and activations in float32 (--dtype float32 in SGLang, torch_dtype=torch.float32 in transformers). This is exactly what you'd get if someone handed you a model and you served it with zero thought about efficiency.

We use Qwen/Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct ($SMALL_MODEL) for this and the next several labs because at FP32 it is ~30GB of weights, comfortably fits on one B200 (183GB) with room for KV cache, and downloads quickly.

What this lab measures

Step What it is What it isolates
1. hf_naive_baseline.py Plain transformers model.generate() in a Python for-loop, one request at a time, FP32 The true floor: no server, no batching, no paged KV cache
2. SGLang FP32, concurrency=1 Same FP32 weights, but behind sglang.launch_server, one request in flight at a time How much do SGLang's fused kernels / scheduler / RadixAttention alone help, even with no batching opportunity?
3. SGLang FP32, concurrency=64 Same server, 64 concurrent requests How much does continuous batching alone add, with precision still unchanged?

Notice precision never changes within this lab -- that axis is lab02. This lab isolates the "just use a real inference engine" axis, which in our experience is often the single biggest lever people forget to pull.

Run it

cd vllm_labs/sglang/lab01_fp32_baseline
./run_lab.sh

Takes ~5-10 minutes (the HF sequential loop is the slow part, by design -- that's the point). Results land in results/lab01_fp32_baseline/ and are appended to results/summary.csv.

Things to look at afterwards

  • results/lab01_fp32_baseline/hf_naive.json -- per-request latency and overall output_throughput (tokens/sec) for the naive loop.
  • results/lab01_fp32_baseline/bench_conc1.log and bench_conc64.log -- console output from sglang.bench_serving, including TTFT (time to first token) and TPOT (time per output token) percentiles.
  • Compare output_throughput_tok_s across the three rows in results/summary.csv for lab=lab01_fp32_baseline.

Expected takeaways

  • SGLang at concurrency=1 should already beat the naive HF loop by a meaningful margin, purely from better attention kernels (FlashInfer) and avoiding Python-loop overhead -- with zero precision or batching changes.
  • SGLang at concurrency=64 should show a dramatically higher output_throughput_tok_s than concurrency=1, at the cost of higher per-request latency (TTFT/TPOT) as requests share GPU time. This throughput/latency trade-off from continuous batching is the central design point of every modern LLM serving engine, including SGLang.
  • Peak GPU memory in the naive HF run vs. what nvidia-smi shows for the SGLang server (check the server log) -- SGLang pre-allocates most of GPU memory in --mem-fraction-static for KV cache up front; the naive loop under-uses memory badly.

Move on to lab02_precision once you've looked at these numbers.

lessons.title: Lab 02 - Precision: FP32 vs FP16 vs BF16
lessons.html:
Goal: isolate the effect of numeric precision alone on memory footprint, throughput, and output quality, holding model, hardware, and load pattern fixed.

Background

B200 (Blackwell) tensor cores deliver dramatically higher FLOPs for bf16/fp16 than for fp32 (and higher still for fp8/fp4, covered in lab03). Halving bytes-per-parameter (4 bytes -> 2 bytes) also halves:

  • The GPU memory needed to hold the weights.
  • The size of the KV cache per token, which means SGLang's memory allocator (--mem-fraction-static) can fit a larger max_running_requests and a deeper RadixAttention prefix-cache tree in the same GPU memory.

That second effect compounds with the first: more concurrent requests fitting in memory means continuous batching has more work to overlap, so throughput gains from precision reduction are often larger than the raw FLOPs ratio would suggest.

bf16 and fp16 have the same bit width (16 bits) but split it differently (bf16: 8 exponent / 7 mantissa bits, matching fp32's dynamic range with less precision; fp16: 5 exponent / 10 mantissa bits, more precision but a much smaller dynamic range that can overflow on some activations). Modern LLMs are almost universally trained and released in bf16 for this reason.

What this lab does

Launches the same $SMALL_MODEL, TP=1, three times with --dtype float32, --dtype bfloat16, --dtype float16, and for each:

  1. Records GPU memory used right after model load.
  2. Grabs one qualitative sample completion (temperature 0, so deterministic) so you can eyeball whether reduced precision visibly changed the answer.
  3. Runs sglang.bench_serving with identical load ($BENCH_NUM_PROMPTS prompts, $BENCH_MAX_CONCURRENCY concurrency) and records throughput/latency.

Run it

cd vllm_labs/sglang/lab02_precision
./run_lab.sh

Expected takeaways

  • bfloat16 and float16 should use roughly half the GPU memory of float32 for weights, and show meaningfully higher output_throughput_tok_s in results/summary.csv.
  • The three qualitative samples in results/lab02_precision/sample_*.txt should be very close in content (Qwen2.5 was trained in bf16, so bf16 is the "native" precision; fp32 is a lossless upcast of those same weights; fp16 can occasionally diverge more due to its narrower dynamic range, though for a 7B chat model at greedy decoding this is usually imperceptible).
  • This is the cheapest possible win in the entire curriculum: one flag change, no retraining, no accuracy-tuning required to go from FP32 to BF16. Always start here before reaching for quantization.

Move on to lab03_quantization for the next rung down: FP8 and INT4.
