lessons.title: Lab 03 - Quantization: FP8 and INT4
lessons.html:
Goal: understand the two flavors of quantization SGLang supports -- online (quantize a full-precision checkpoint at load time) and offline / pre-quantized (load someone else's already-quantized checkpoint) -- and see their memory/throughput/quality trade-offs relative to bf16.

Background

  • FP8 (--quantization fp8): SGLang casts the bf16 weights to FP8 (E4M3) on the fly when the server starts. B200's tensor cores have native FP8 matmul support (2x the FLOPs of bf16 on the same silicon), so this is typically the best throughput-per-accuracy-lost trade available on Blackwell. No calibration dataset or offline step required.
  • AWQ (Activation-aware Weight Quantization) / GPTQ: both quantize weights down to INT4, but need an offline calibration pass against sample data to decide how to round weights with minimal output error. We use community pre-quantized checkpoints (Qwen/Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct-AWQ and -GPTQ-Int4) so this lab doesn't need to run its own calibration job -- SGLang auto-detects the quantization method from the checkpoint's config.json, so you do not pass --quantization for these.
  • Weight-only INT4 quantization keeps activations/KV-cache at higher precision and dequantizes weights on the fly during the matmul, so it saves memory more than it saves compute -- useful when you're memory-bound rather than compute-bound.

What this lab does

Runs four server configurations against the same benchmark load:

  1. bf16-baseline -- re-measured here so this lab stands on its own.
  2. fp8-online -- $SMALL_MODEL loaded with --quantization fp8.
  3. awq-int4 -- $AWQ_MODEL (pre-quantized, auto-detected).
  4. gptq-int4 -- $GPTQ_MODEL (pre-quantized, auto-detected).

For each: GPU memory footprint, one deterministic qualitative sample, and a full bench_serving throughput/latency run.

Run it

cd vllm_labs/sglang/lab03_quantization
./run_lab.sh

Expected takeaways

  • Memory: bf16 > fp8 > awq-int4 ~= gptq-int4, roughly in a 4 : 2 : 1 : 1 ratio for weights (KV cache size is unaffected by weight quantization, so total memory savings will be somewhat less dramatic than a pure 4x).
  • Throughput: on B200, fp8-online should show a clear throughput win over bf16-baseline with a barely perceptible quality difference in sample_fp8-online.txt vs sample_bf16-baseline.txt. INT4 methods often show even higher throughput at low/medium concurrency (memory-bandwidth bound decode phase moves less data per token), but the gap narrows or can even reverse at very high concurrency where compute-bound prefill dominates and dequantization overhead starts to matter.
  • Read all four sample_*.txt files side by side. This is the most important habit to build for production quantization work: never ship a quantized model without eyeballing (and ideally running a proper eval harness against) its outputs.

Next: lab04_tensor_parallelism moves from "shrink the model" to "spread the model across more GPUs."

lessons.title: Lab 04 - Tensor Parallelism (TP) Scaling
lessons.html:
Goal: measure how throughput scales as you shard a model's weights across more GPUs with --tp, and understand why that scaling is sub-linear.

Background

Tensor parallelism splits individual weight matrices (attention QKVO projections, MLP up/down projections) across GPUs, so each GPU only holds 1/TP of the parameters and does 1/TP of the matmul FLOPs for those layers. After each attention block and each MLP block, the partial results must be combined with an all-reduce across the TP group before the next layer can run. That all-reduce is pure communication overhead with no useful compute -- it's the tax you pay for splitting the model.

On this node, all 8 B200s should be NVLink-connected (verify with nvidia-smi topo -m), which is exactly the hardware TP wants: low-latency, high-bandwidth interconnect for those frequent, small-ish all-reduces. Multi-node TP over Ethernet/InfiniBand is far more sensitive to this overhead -- generally avoid TP across nodes if you can, and prefer it within a node.

We use $MID_MODEL (Qwen2.5-32B-Instruct, bf16, ~65GB) specifically because it fits on one B200 already. That means TP=1 is a valid, meaningful baseline, and any speedup at TP=2/4/8 reflects real parallel scaling -- not "it didn't even fit before."

What this lab does

Launches the same model at --tp 1, --tp 2, --tp 4, --tp 8 (skipping sizes larger than the GPUs you have available), and for each, runs bench_serving with an identical, fixed request load (same --num-prompts, same --max-concurrency). Holding load fixed is what makes the comparison a clean measurement of parallel-compute scaling rather than "more GPUs -> more room for concurrent requests" (a real and separate benefit you'd also chase in production, just not what we're isolating here).

Run it

cd vllm_labs/sglang/lab04_tensor_parallelism
./run_lab.sh

This needs multiple GPUs to see the interesting part; it will auto-skip TP sizes beyond what nvidia-smi reports. On your 8xB200 node it will run all four configurations.

Expected takeaways

  • Total throughput should increase from TP=1 to TP=8, but per-GPU throughput (total_throughput / TP) should decrease as TP grows -- the script prints a "scaling efficiency" table making this explicit.
  • The drop-off is the NCCL all-reduce tax. It grows with TP size (more ranks to synchronize) and shrinks relative to compute as the model gets bigger (more FLOPs to amortize the fixed communication cost against) -- this is why TP is usually reserved for models that don't fit on fewer GPUs, or where you specifically need the lower per-request latency that splitting compute across more GPUs buys you.
  • Compare TTFT (median_ttft_ms) across TP sizes too: TP mainly helps latency per request (the prefill/decode for one sequence is now spread over more GPUs), which is a different axis from the throughput-via-batching win you saw in lab01. Production sizing is a joint decision over both.

Next: lab05_radix_attention looks at SGLang's signature feature -- RadixAttention prefix caching -- which needs no extra GPUs at all.

lessons.title: Lab 05 - RadixAttention: Automatic Prefix Caching
lessons.html:
Goal: see, quantitatively, why RadixAttention is SGLang's headline feature: automatic reuse of KV cache across requests that share a token prefix, with zero application-level changes.

Background

Every LLM request starts with a "prefill" phase (process the whole input prompt to build its KV cache) followed by a "decode" phase (generate output tokens one at a time, extending that KV cache). Prefill cost scales with prompt length -- for a workload with long, repeated system prompts (chat assistants, RAG pipelines, few-shot prompting, agent scaffolding), most GPUs end up repeatedly re-computing KV cache for tokens that are byte-for-byte identical to what a previous request already computed.

SGLang's RadixAttention stores every request's KV cache pages in a radix tree (a trie) keyed by token id sequence. When a new request arrives, SGLang walks the tree to find the longest matching prefix already cached, reuses that KV cache directly, and only computes the (usually much shorter) suffix that's actually new. This is on by default -- no code changes, no special client-side caching logic, it just works based on token-level prefix matching.

What this lab does

Uses sglang.bench_serving --dataset-name generated-shared-prefix, a built-in synthetic workload generator that creates $GSP_NUM_GROUPS distinct "system prompts" (~$GSP_SYSTEM_PROMPT_LEN tokens each) and issues $GSP_PROMPTS_PER_GROUP different short questions against each one -- e.g. 8 groups x 32 questions = 256 requests, but only 8 unique ~2048-token prefixes.

Runs this workload twice against $SMALL_MODEL:

  1. radix-cache-enabled -- SGLang's default.
  2. radix-cache-disabled -- launched with --disable-radix-cache, which forces every request to prefill its full prompt from scratch even if an identical prefix was just processed.

Run it

cd vllm_labs/sglang/lab05_radix_attention
./run_lab.sh

Expected takeaways

  • median_ttft_ms (time to first token) should be dramatically lower with RadixAttention enabled: after the first request in each group "warms" the cache for that system prompt, every subsequent request in the same group only needs to prefill the short, unique question -- not the full ~2048-token shared prefix.
  • output_throughput_tok_s should also be higher with caching enabled, since GPU time that would have been spent redundantly re-prefilling identical tokens is instead available for decoding other requests.
  • This benefit is "free" -- it required zero changes to how you structure requests, as long as your client sends the same token sequence for the shared portion (same system prompt text, same tokenizer, no non-deterministic templating). It's why designing your prompts to put static/shared content first and per-request/dynamic content last is a best practice for any RadixAttention-based server.
  • Try increasing GSP_SYSTEM_PROMPT_LEN (e.g. GSP_SYSTEM_PROMPT_LEN=8192 ./run_lab.sh) to see the gap widen further -- the longer the shared prefix relative to the unique suffix, the bigger RadixAttention's win.

Next: lab06_scheduling_batching tunes the knobs that control how SGLang's continuous batching scheduler packs requests together.

lessons.title: Lab 06 - Continuous Batching & Scheduler Knobs
lessons.html:
Goal: understand the three scheduler settings that most affect throughput/latency trade-offs once RadixAttention and precision are already handled: overlap scheduling, chunked prefill, and queue ordering policy.

Background

SGLang's scheduler runs a loop: at every iteration, decide which requests (new prefills and in-flight decodes) to run together as one GPU batch. Three knobs shape this:

  • Overlap scheduling (on by default): the CPU thread that decides the next batch runs concurrently with the GPU executing the current batch, instead of waiting for the GPU to finish first. This hides scheduling and Python-side overhead behind GPU compute -- pure upside on GPUs with fast CPUs, at the cost of one extra batch of "lookahead" latency for aborts/rate limiting to take effect.
  • Chunked prefill (--chunked-prefill-size N): normally, prefilling a very long prompt is one big matmul-heavy step. If a 4096-token prompt needs prefilling right when 30 other requests are mid-decode, the naive approach makes those 30 requests wait for the entire prefill to finish. Chunked prefill splits long prefills into N-token pieces and interleaves them with other requests' decode steps, trading a bit of total throughput for dramatically better tail latency.
  • Schedule policy (--schedule-policy): controls which queued request is picked next. fcfs (first-come-first-served) is simple and fair. lpm (longest-prefix-match) instead prioritizes requests that share a RadixAttention prefix with what's currently cached/running, improving cache locality (fewer evictions, more reuse) under prefix-heavy traffic at some cost to strict request-arrival fairness.

What this lab does

Three back-to-back A/B comparisons, each holding everything else fixed:

  • [A] --disable-overlap-schedule off vs on, random workload.
  • [B] --chunked-prefill-size -1 (disabled) vs 2048 (enabled), with 4096-token input prompts, so a real prefill/decode contention scenario actually occurs.
  • [C] --schedule-policy fcfs vs lpm, on the same generated-shared-prefix workload from lab05.

Run it

cd vllm_labs/sglang/lab06_scheduling_batching
./run_lab.sh

Expected takeaways

  • [A] Overlap scheduling should give a small, consistent throughput/TPOT improvement with no real downside -- there's rarely a reason to disable it in production; it exists mainly as a debugging knob.
  • [B] Look at p99_ttft_ms in results/lab06_scheduling_batching/bench_chunked_off.log vs bench_chunked_on.log: disabling chunked prefill should show occasional very high tail latencies for requests unlucky enough to be queued behind a long prompt's prefill. Total throughput may be similar or even slightly higher without chunking (less scheduling overhead) -- this is a genuine throughput-vs-tail-latency trade-off, not a strict win either way.
  • [C] lpm should match or beat fcfs on throughput/TTFT for the prefix-heavy workload, since it actively schedules cache-friendly requests together instead of processing strictly in arrival order.
  • None of these knobs require touching the model or its weights at all -- they're pure serving-layer tuning, and usually the first place to look before reaching for more GPUs or a smaller model.

Next: lab07_cuda_graph_torch_compile looks at kernel-launch-level optimizations: CUDA graphs and torch.compile.

lessons.title: Lab 07 - CUDA Graphs & torch.compile
lessons.html:
Goal: understand kernel-launch-overhead optimizations, which matter most for the decode phase of serving (many cheap, repetitive steps).

Background

  • CUDA graphs: capture the full sequence of GPU kernel launches for a given batch shape once, then replay the whole graph with a single lightweight API call on every subsequent step, instead of re-dispatching each kernel individually from Python/C++ every time. This eliminates per-kernel CPU launch overhead, which matters a lot during decode (many small kernels, once per token, per request in the batch) and much less during prefill (a handful of large matmuls that are compute-bound regardless of launch overhead). SGLang captures graphs for a set of common batch sizes at server startup (you'll see a "Capturing cuda graph" log line listing batch sizes) and falls back to eager execution for uncaptured shapes.
  • torch.compile: PyTorch's JIT compiler traces the model's forward pass and generates fused, specialized kernels (via TorchInductor) for it. This is complementary to CUDA graphs (which just replay whatever kernels already exist) since it can create better kernels in the first place. SGLang's docs currently mark --enable-torch-compile as an experimental, lightly-maintained feature that can fail for some model/version combinations -- this lab treats it as best-effort and continues even if it fails to start.

What this lab does

Three server configurations against $SMALL_MODEL, benchmarked with a decode-heavy workload (long output length, moderate concurrency, so per-step overhead is a meaningful fraction of total time):

  1. cuda-graph-on -- SGLang's default.
  2. cuda-graph-off -- --cuda-graph-backend-decode disabled --cuda-graph-backend-prefill disabled.
  3. torch-compile-on -- --enable-torch-compile (skipped automatically if it fails to start on your SGLang version).

Run it

cd vllm_labs/sglang/lab07_cuda_graph_torch_compile
./run_lab.sh

Startup for the CUDA-graph-enabled configurations takes noticeably longer than a normal server start -- SGLang is capturing graphs for a range of batch sizes before it reports healthy. Watch the server logs (results/lab07_cuda_graph_torch_compile/server_*.log) to see this happen.

Expected takeaways

  • median_tpot_ms (time per output token = decode step cost) should be visibly higher with CUDA graphs disabled -- this is the metric CUDA graphs target directly.
  • median_ttft_ms (time to first token = prefill cost) should barely move between the two CUDA-graph configurations, confirming that prefill is matmul-bound rather than launch-overhead-bound.
  • If the torch-compile-on row is present in results/summary.csv, compare median_tpot_ms against cuda-graph-on -- gains beyond what CUDA graphs already provide are usually modest for a 7B model at these batch sizes, since CUDA graphs already remove most launch overhead; torch.compile mainly helps when there's additional kernel-fusion opportunity (e.g. fusing normalization + activation ops) that raw graph replay can't provide.

Next: lab08_speculative_decoding attacks the decode phase from a completely different angle -- generating multiple tokens per forward pass.

lessons.title: Lab 08 - Speculative Decoding (N-gram)
lessons.html:
Goal: understand how speculative decoding turns "1 forward pass = 1 token" into "1 forward pass = several tokens (when the guesses are right)", using a method that needs zero extra models to demonstrate.

Background

Decoding is memory-bandwidth bound: generating one token means reading the entire model's weights (and KV cache) from HBM for a batch that's often small relative to the GPU's compute capacity. Speculative decoding exploits this by having a cheap "drafter" propose several candidate future tokens, then running one forward pass of the real target model to verify all of them simultaneously (a form of prefill-shaped, parallel computation). Since that verification pass costs about the same as generating a single token normally, every additional accepted draft token is close to free.

Common drafters:

  • EAGLE / EAGLE3: a small, separately-trained neural network predicts draft tokens using the target model's own hidden states. Highest quality speedups, but requires a compatible pretrained EAGLE checkpoint for your exact target model (not always available, and out of scope for a zero-extra-downloads lab).
  • STANDALONE: use a smaller full LLM as the drafter (e.g. a 1B model drafting for a 70B target). Needs a second model server-side.
  • NGRAM (what we use here): no model at all. SGLang keeps a cache of recently-seen token n-grams (from the prompt and from what's already been generated) and proposes continuations by pattern-matching against it. Zero setup cost, but only helps when output has local redundancy: copying or lightly editing input text, structured/repetitive formats, code with repeated tokens, etc. For open-ended creative generation the hit rate (and thus the speedup) is much smaller.

What this lab does

Two server configurations against $SMALL_MODEL:

  1. no-spec -- plain baseline.
  2. ngram-spec -- --speculative-algorithm NGRAM --speculative-num-draft-tokens 16 --speculative-ngram-max-bfs-breadth 10.

For each, two benchmarks:

  • general: bench_serving with generic random-content prompts (natural language has some redundancy, so expect a modest win).
  • repetitive: repetitive_task_client.py sends prompts explicitly designed to produce highly redundant output (numbered lists, verbatim repetition, tables) -- the best case for n-gram speculation.

Run it

cd vllm_labs/sglang/lab08_speculative_decoding
./run_lab.sh

Note: NGRAM speculative decoding is CUDA-only and automatically disables the overlap scheduler and mixed chunked prefill internally (SGLang handles this for you; you don't need extra flags) -- so part of what you measure here also reflects that trade-off, not purely the speculative-decoding win.

Expected takeaways

  • ngram-spec-general vs no-spec-general: expect a real but modest output_throughput_tok_s improvement.
  • ngram-spec-repetitive vs no-spec-repetitive: expect a much larger improvement -- this is the workload shape where speculative decoding earns its keep in production (e.g. code-editing assistants, "reformat this data" tools, autocomplete).
  • Check the server log (server_ngram.log) for any lines mentioning acceptance rate / accept length if your SGLang version logs them -- higher accepted-tokens-per-step directly explains the throughput gain.
  • If you have access to a compatible EAGLE checkpoint for your target model in a real deployment, prefer it over NGRAM: EAGLE's learned drafter generalizes far better across content types than n-gram matching.

lessons.title: Lab 09 - Structured Output / Grammar-Guided Decoding
lessons.html:
Goal: measure the reliability gain and latency cost of enforcing a JSON Schema on model output via SGLang's grammar backend, versus just asking nicely in the prompt.

Background

LLMs are surprisingly good at producing JSON when asked, but "surprisingly good" isn't "guaranteed" -- extra prose before/after the JSON, trailing commas, unescaped quotes, or truncated output at max_tokens are all common failure modes that show up more often than you'd like in production at scale.

SGLang's grammar backends (default: xgrammar, also supports outlines and llguidance) solve this differently: at every decoding step, they compute a token mask that only allows tokens which keep the output on a path consistent with your schema (compiled to a pushdown automaton / FSM), then apply that mask to the logits before sampling. The model literally cannot emit a token that would break the schema. This costs some extra per-step CPU/GPU work to compute and apply the mask, which we measure here.

What this lab does

Launches $SMALL_MODEL once with --grammar-backend xgrammar, then:

  1. Unconstrained: json_schema_client.py --constrained false asks the model in plain English to "respond with only a JSON object" and checks how often the raw output actually parses as valid JSON with the required fields.
  2. Constrained: same task, same prompts, but with response_format={"type": "json_schema", ...} set on the request, letting SGLang enforce the schema.
  3. An optional throughput-under-load comparison via bench_serving (skipped automatically if your SGLang version's bench_serving doesn't expose a --json-schema flag -- check the console output).

Run it

cd vllm_labs/sglang/lab09_structured_output
./run_lab.sh

Expected takeaways

  • constrained should show num_valid_json / num_requests at or very close to 100%. unconstrained will likely show at least one failure (extra commentary text, a stray field, wrong type for age, etc.) even though the model is generally well-behaved -- this gap is exactly why production extraction/tool-calling pipelines should use constrained decoding instead of prompt-and-pray plus a JSON parser wrapped in retry logic.
  • mean_latency_s should be modestly higher for the constrained case (extra grammar-mask computation per step), but usually far cheaper than the latency of a failed parse + retry round-trip would have been.
  • If the load-test rows are present in results/summary.csv, compare median_tpot_ms between plain-decoding-load and constrained-decoding-load to see the per-token overhead in a concurrent, throughput-oriented setting rather than one-request-at-a-time.

lessons.title: Lab 10 - Mixture-of-Experts: Expert Parallelism & DP Attention
lessons.html:
Goal: understand the two parallelism strategies unique to Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models, and why plain tensor parallelism is often not the best fit for them.

Background

$MOE_MODEL (Qwen3-30B-A3B) is a MoE model: it has ~30B total parameters organized into many small expert MLPs, but a per-token router activates only a handful of experts per forward pass (~3B "active" parameters worth of compute per token). This changes the parallelism trade-offs vs a dense model like the ones in labs 01-04:

  • Plain TP shards every expert's weight matrix across all GPUs (same as it would for a dense model's single MLP). Simple, but wasteful: each GPU stores and computes against a slice of experts that a given token may not have even been routed to.
  • Expert Parallelism (EP) instead places whole experts on specific GPUs, and uses an all-to-all communication step to route each token's hidden state to whichever GPU(s) hold its selected expert(s), then another all-to-all to bring results back. In SGLang, --ep "subdivides" the TP group (--tp 8 --ep 8 uses the 8-GPU TP group to host 8 distinct expert shards). This avoids redundant expert compute, at the cost of all-to-all communication instead of all-reduce.
  • DP Attention (--enable-dp-attention --dp-size N) targets a different inefficiency: attention layers are relatively small compared to a MoE model's total FLOPs, so tensor-parallelizing them (which requires an all-reduce and duplicates KV cache management overhead across ranks) is wasteful. DP attention instead runs each GPU's attention layers on its own independent slice of requests (true data parallelism, no cross-GPU communication for attention), while the larger FFN/expert layers still use TP or EP.

A real, current gotcha (worth knowing about)

Combining DP-attention with EP>1 at the same time has an open, known correctness bug on bf16 MoE checkpoints that aren't using the DeepEP kernel path (see sgl-project/sglang#23729). Since $MOE_MODEL is bf16, this lab deliberately measures EP and DP attention separately rather than stacking them, and this README calls that decision out explicitly. The combined "DPA + EP" recipe is the documented, recommended production setup for models like DeepSeek-V3 when running an FP8 checkpoint with --moe-a2a-backend deepep -- but "the docs say to combine these flags" and "this specific model+precision+version combination actually works correctly" are different claims, and the second one is always worth verifying yourself before shipping. This is a good general lesson for working with a fast-moving inference engine: always sanity-check output quality (not just throughput numbers) after stacking multiple advanced parallelism flags.

What this lab does

Requires all 8 GPUs. Runs $MOE_MODEL three ways against identical benchmark load:

  1. tp8-baseline -- --tp 8.
  2. tp8-ep8 -- --tp 8 --ep 8.
  3. tp8-dp8-attention -- --tp 8 --dp-size 8 --enable-dp-attention.

Run it

cd vllm_labs/sglang/lab10_moe_expert_parallel
./run_lab.sh

Expected takeaways

  • tp8-ep8 should generally outperform tp8-baseline for this model, since it eliminates redundant per-GPU expert computation -- the gap should be larger at higher concurrency (more tokens per all-to-all round = better amortized communication cost) and smaller (or even reversed) at very low concurrency.
  • tp8-dp8-attention should show its benefit mainly in memory efficiency (no duplicated KV cache management across the attention TP group) and can particularly help at high concurrency / long context, where attention's KV cache footprint becomes a bigger fraction of total memory pressure.
  • Try re-running with BENCH_MAX_CONCURRENCY=16 ./run_lab.sh and then BENCH_MAX_CONCURRENCY=128 ./run_lab.sh to see how the ranking between these three strategies shifts with load -- there is no universally "best" MoE parallelism strategy independent of your expected traffic pattern.

Next: lab11_capstone combines the single best setting from each earlier lab into one "production recipe" server and measures the cumulative speedup versus lab01's naive FP32 baseline.

lessons.title: Lab 11 - Capstone: Stack the Wins
lessons.html:
Goal: combine the broadly-applicable optimizations from the earlier labs into one server configuration, and put a single number on the total speedup from "naive FP32, one request at a time" to "SGLang, tuned."

Prerequisite

Run lab01_fp32_baseline at least once before this lab -- the final comparison table reads its results from results/summary.csv. If you haven't run every lab, that's fine; this lab still measures the optimized recipe's absolute numbers, it just can't print every intermediate comparison row.

The recipe

python -m sglang.launch_server \
  --model-path Qwen/Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct \
  --tp 1 \
  --dtype bfloat16 \
  --quantization fp8

Notice what's not an explicit flag here: RadixAttention prefix caching, continuous batching with the overlap scheduler, chunked prefill, and CUDA graph capture are all on by default in SGLang. The only things this recipe adds explicitly on top of an out-of-the-box launch are the precision (bf16 base + fp8 quantization) choices from labs 02-03. That's deliberate: this capstone's point is that most of SGLang's value is already there the moment you use it as your serving engine (lab01's lesson), and the highest -leverage manual choice on top of that is picking the right numeric precision for your hardware (labs 02-03).

Deliberately left out of the default recipe, because their benefit is workload-dependent rather than universal:

  • Speculative decoding (lab08) -- big win for repetitive/structured output, smaller for open-ended generation.
  • Tensor/expert/data parallelism (labs 04, 10) -- only relevant once a model doesn't fit on (or isn't fast enough on) one GPU.
  • Non-default scheduler tuning (lab06) -- lpm scheduling only helps prefix-heavy traffic; chunked prefill's default is already reasonable for most workloads.

What this lab does

  1. Launches the recipe above.
  2. Benchmarks it at concurrency=1 (directly comparable to lab01's naive HF loop and naive SGLang-FP32-concurrency=1 numbers) and at concurrency=$BENCH_MAX_CONCURRENCY (comparable to lab01's SGLang-FP32 batching number).
  3. Prints a final comparison table with speedup multipliers relative to the naive HF baseline.
  4. Calls common/plot_results.py to render bar charts across every lab you've run into results/plots/.

Run it

cd vllm_labs/sglang/lab11_capstone
./run_lab.sh

Expected takeaways

  • The concurrency=1 comparison isolates the pure "better engine + better precision" win with no batching involved -- expect this alone to be a multi-x speedup over the naive HF loop.
  • The concurrency=$BENCH_MAX_CONCURRENCY comparison additionally captures continuous batching's throughput multiplier on top of that -- expect this to be the largest speedup number in the whole curriculum.
  • Look at results/plots/throughput.png for a single chart spanning every lab you've run, from the naive FP32 baseline all the way to this recipe.
  • The real lesson: optimization is not one silver bullet, it's a stack of mostly-independent, mostly-compatible levers (engine choice, precision, parallelism, scheduling, caching, speculative decoding), and the right combination depends on your model size, hardware, and traffic pattern -- which is exactly why each lab isolated one lever at a time instead of just handing you a single "optimal" config.

You've now worked through the full FP32-to-optimized-serving journey on SGLang. Re-run any lab with different $SMALL_MODEL / $MID_MODEL / $MOE_MODEL values, different BENCH_* load parameters, or on a different GPU count to build intuition for how these trade-offs shift.

lessons.title: Lab 12: Attention backends on Blackwell
lessons.html:
Concept

The attention kernel is the one part of the transformer forward pass whose cost grows with context length, and it is also the part that reads the paged KV cache. SGLang exposes the kernel library as a server argument:

python -m sglang.launch_server --model-path Qwen/Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct --attention-backend fa4
# or per phase:
python -m sglang.launch_server ... --prefill-attention-backend fa4 --decode-attention-backend trtllm_mha

Current choices include triton, torch_native, flex_attention, fa3, fa4, flashinfer, trtllm_mha, and MLA-specific backends (flashmla, trtllm_mla, cutedsl_mla, ...) for DeepSeek-style models. On B200 the four worth comparing for a GQA model are:

Backend What it is
fa4 FlashAttention 4, written in CuTe-DSL for Blackwell's tensor memory (TMEM) and 2-CTA MMA.
flashinfer FlashInfer's paged attention (JIT-compiled, plan/run split for CUDA graphs).
trtllm_mha TensorRT-LLM's hand-tuned Blackwell MHA kernels, exposed via FlashInfer.
triton Portable Triton kernels - the reference point.

What this lab does

For each backend: start the server, run a prefill-heavy workload (4000 in / 32 out, concurrency 32) and a decode-heavy workload (128 in / 512 out, concurrency 4), stop the server. A backend that is not supported by your SGLang build is skipped.

lessons.title: Lab 13: HiCache - hierarchical KV cache (GPU -> CPU)
lessons.html:
Concept

RadixAttention (Lab 05) reuses KV cache for shared prefixes, but only while those prefixes are still resident in GPU memory. Real traffic often has a working set of prefixes much larger than HBM: thousands of tenants with their own system prompts, RAG over many documents, long multi-turn agent sessions that come back minutes later. Once the radix tree evicts a prefix, the next request pays the full prefill again.

HiCache puts a host-memory tier (and optionally a storage tier such as 3FS, Mooncake or a file system via --hicache-storage-backend) behind the radix tree:

  • On eviction, KV pages are copied to pinned CPU RAM instead of dropped (--hicache-write-policy write_through copies eagerly, write_back copies only on eviction).
  • On a hit in the host tier, pages are prefetched back to the GPU over PCIe/C2C - far cheaper than recomputing thousands of tokens of prefill.
  • --hicache-size sets the host tier in GB per TP rank (or --hicache-ratio as a multiple of the GPU pool).

This is SGLang's equivalent of vLLM's OffloadingConnector / LMCache, and it is exactly what llm-d's tiered prefix cache guide enables for SGLang pods.

What this lab does

Shrinks the GPU KV pool (--mem-fraction-static 0.2) and sends a generated-shared-prefix workload whose distinct prefixes (~524K tokens) exceed it. Three runs:

  1. no-prefix-cache - --disable-radix-cache (floor).
  2. radix-gpu-only - default RadixAttention, GPU tier only.
  3. radix-plus-hicache - --enable-hierarchical-cache --hicache-size 100.

Run it

cd sglang/lab13_hierarchical_cache && ./run_lab.sh

What to look for

  • median_ttft_ms: HiCache should sit close to what lab05 shows for a fully-resident cache, while GPU-only radix falls back towards the no-cache floor.
  • Server log of the HiCache run: host-tier hit/load statistics.
  • The KV math in the script header - redo it for your model (layers x KV heads x head_dim x 2 x bytes) to size GPU vs host tiers.

lessons.title: llm-d track overview
lessons.html:
The vLLM and SGLang tracks make a single model server fast. This track is about what happens when you run many of them behind one endpoint: which replica should serve each request, how to split prefill from decode, how to keep KV cache across tiers and replicas, how to keep tenants from hurting each other, and how to scale the fleet with demand.

Everything targets the same single 8xB200 node, with upstream llm-d v1.0 components (router/EPP, Envoy, vLLM v0.31.0, SGLang v0.5.22).

# Lab Runs on What it teaches

02 lab02_scheduler_ablation Docker Filters/scorers/pickers, affinity vs load, live pool changes
03 lab03_flow_control Docker Fair queuing in the router: quiet vs noisy tenant

lessons.title: llm-d Lab 00: Setup
lessons.html:
What llm-d is

llm-d (v1.0, CNCF sandbox) is a Kubernetes-native distributed inference stack built around vLLM and SGLang rather than replacing them. vLLM/SGLang make one replica fast; llm-d makes a fleet of replicas fast and cheap:

  • llm-d Router = a proxy (Envoy, or agentgateway) + the EPP (Endpoint Picker), an Envoy ext_proc gRPC service that decides which model-server replica gets each request using live state: queue depth, KV cache utilization, which replica already caches this prompt's prefix, predicted latency.
  • InferencePool (Gateway API Inference Extension CRD) = the set of model-server pods the EPP may pick from.
  • Well-lit paths: tested recipes for intelligent scheduling, prefill/decode disaggregation, precise prefix-cache routing, tiered KV cache, wide expert parallelism, flow control and autoscaling.

Two ways to run the labs on one 8xB200 box

  1. No Kubernetes (labs 01-06): vLLM replicas, the EPP and Envoy run as Docker containers on the host network. The EPP reads its replica list from a YAML file (file-discovery plugin) instead of watching an InferencePool. This is an upstream-supported deployment and is the fastest way to see routing decisions.
  2. Kubernetes (labs 07-09): a single-node minikube cluster with GPU passthrough, then the upstream guides deployed unchanged with helm + kustomize.

What this lab does

  • Verifies Docker can start GPU containers (NVIDIA Container Toolkit).
  • Pulls the images the guides pin: vllm/vllm-openai:v0.31.0, envoyproxy/envoy:distroless-v1.33.2, ghcr.io/llm-d/llm-d-router-endpoint-picker, lmsysorg/sglang:v0.5.22.
  • Downloads Qwen/Qwen3-32B (routing labs), openai/gpt-oss-120b (P/D, the upstream guide's model) and Qwen/Qwen3-30B-A3B (wide-EP) into $HF_HOME.
  • Clones llm-d/llm-d into llmd/.upstream/llm-d for the Kubernetes labs.

Run it

cd llmd/lab00_setup
export HF_TOKEN=hf_...            # recommended
./run_lab.sh                      # add --with-k8s-tools for labs 07-09

Configuration

All knobs live in llmd/common/env.sh and can be overridden from the environment: LLMD_MODEL, LLMD_TP, LLMD_REPLICAS, image tags, ROUTER_EPP_VERSION, LLMD_UPSTREAM_REF, HF_HOME.

lessons.title: llm-d Lab 01: Why LLM traffic needs an inference-aware router
lessons.html:
Concept

A classic load balancer assumes requests are roughly interchangeable and replicas are stateless. LLM serving breaks both assumptions:

  • Requests differ by orders of magnitude. A 50-token chat turn and a 30,000-token RAG prompt cost wildly different amounts of prefill compute, and output length is unknown up front. "Number of open connections" is a poor proxy for load.
  • Replicas are stateful. Each vLLM replica holds a prefix cache (KV blocks for prompts it has seen). Sending a request to the replica that already holds its 6,000-token system prompt skips that prefill entirely. Sending it anywhere else recomputes it and evicts something useful.

The llm-d EPP (Endpoint Picker) is plugged into Envoy as an ext_proc filter. For every request Envoy streams the headers/body to the EPP, which runs a filter → score → pick pipeline over the replicas and answers with the chosen endpoint in the x-gateway-destination-endpoint header; Envoy's ORIGINAL_DST cluster then forwards the request there.

The no-Kubernetes optimized-baseline profile used here combines:

Scorer Weight Signal
prefix-cache-scorer 3 How much of this prompt's prefix the EPP predicts is cached on each replica (it hashes prompt blocks and remembers where it sent them).
queue-scorer 2 Waiting requests per replica, scraped from vLLM /metrics.
kv-cache-utilization-scorer 2 KV-cache memory pressure per replica.
no-hit-lru-scorer 2 For prompts with no cache hit anywhere, spread them to the least-recently-used replica so new prefixes don't pile up.

Setup

client (loadgen.py) ──> Envoy :8081 ──ext_proc──> EPP :9002
                           │                       │ scrapes /metrics
                           └──> vllm-0 :8000  (GPUs 0,1)
                                vllm-1 :8001  (GPUs 2,3)
                                vllm-2 :8002  (GPUs 4,5)
                                vllm-3 :8003  (GPUs 6,7)

The EPP gets its replica list from endpoints.yaml (file discovery). The configs are copied verbatim from upstream guides/no-kubernetes-deployment/router/.

Workload

48 "tenants", each with a ~6,000-token system prompt, sending 960 short questions in random order at concurrency 96 (loadgen.py --workload shared-prefix). The total prefix working set (~290K tokens) fits in the pool's combined KV cache only if each prefix lives on one replica.

Run it

cd llmd/lab01_router_basics && ./run_lab.sh
# smaller model / more replicas:
LLMD_MODEL=meta-llama/Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct LLMD_TP=1 LLMD_REPLICAS=8 ./run_lab.sh

What to look for

  • prefix_hit_rate: round-robin should be far below the EPP.
  • ttft_p50_ms / ttft_p99_ms: the EPP should cut TTFT sharply.
  • max_replica_share: should stay close to 0.25 with the EPP; prefix affinity without load awareness would create hot replicas (see lab 02).
  • Least-request vs round-robin: load awareness alone fixes queueing imbalance but not cache misses.

lessons.title: llm-d Lab 02: Inside the scheduler - filters, scorers, pickers
lessons.html:
Concept

For each request the EPP runs one or more scheduling profiles. A profile is a pipeline:

  1. Filters drop ineligible endpoints (wrong role in P/D, unhealthy, saturated, not cache-warm enough).
  2. Scorers give each remaining endpoint a score in [0, 1]; scores are combined with the configured weights.
  3. A picker chooses (max-score-picker, weighted-random-picker, ...).

Data feeding the scorers comes from producers and the data layer: scraped model-server metrics (metrics-data-source + core-metrics-extractor: queue length, KV-cache usage, running requests), in-flight load tracked by the EPP itself (inflight-load-producer), and the prefix index (approx-prefix-cache-producer, or exact KV events in the precise prefix-cache path).

Two production profiles ship upstream:

  • No-Kubernetes optimized baseline: prefix-cache-scorer (3) + queue-scorer (2) + kv-cache-utilization-scorer (2) + no-hit-lru-scorer (2).
  • v1.0 optimized baseline (Kubernetes guide): prefix-cache-affinity-filter + token-load-scorer. The filter keeps each prefix group on its cache-warm endpoints until their estimated prefill backlog exceeds what they can absorb (peakPrefillThroughput, calibrated per model/accelerator); then the token-load scorer picks the endpoint with the fewest queued prompt tokens.

What this lab does

  1. Runs a skewed shared-prefix workload (6 hot groups, concurrency 128) under four EPP configs: load-only, prefix-only, optimized-baseline, affinity-token-load (configs in llmd/configs/epp/).
  2. Live pool change: while traffic flows, rewrites endpoints.yaml (atomic rename) with one replica fewer. The EPP's file watcher reloads the pool and stops routing to the drained replica - the same mechanism a Kubernetes InferencePool gives you via pod readiness.

Run it

cd llmd/lab02_scheduler_ablation && ./run_lab.sh

What to look for

  • The tension between cache affinity and load balance: prefix-only wins on prefix_hit_rate but loses on ttft_p99_ms and max_replica_share; load-only is the reverse; the combined profiles should get most of both.
  • Calibration: the affinity filter's default peakPrefillThroughput (15928 tokens/s) was measured for Qwen3-32B TP=2 on H100. A B200 has ~2x the prefill throughput, so the filter spills too early. Re-measure with upstream guides/recipes/router/calibration and set it in configs/epp/affinity-token-load.yaml.
  • epp-*.log: per-request scheduling decisions at --v=2.

lessons.title: llm-d Lab 03: Flow control and multi-tenancy
lessons.html:
Concept

When offered load exceeds capacity, requests queue somewhere. Without flow control they queue inside each vLLM replica's scheduler, which is FIFO across all users: a batch job that dumps 2,000 requests makes every interactive user wait behind it. Once a request is committed to a replica's queue it is also stuck there even if another replica frees up first.

llm-d Flow Control moves the queue into the router:

  • Each request is classified into a flow = fairness id (x-llm-d-inference-fairness-id header, e.g. tenant) + priority (from the x-llm-d-inference-objective header, resolved via InferenceObjective resources on Kubernetes).
  • Flows live in priority bands. Each dispatch cycle serves the highest band first, rotates between tenants inside a band (fairness policy, e.g. round-robin) and orders requests within a flow (ordering policy, e.g. FCFS or SLO-aware).
  • A saturation detector (concurrency-detector: max in-flight requests per replica) gates dispatch. While the pool is saturated, requests wait in the EPP; when capacity frees up they go to the best replica at that moment ("no-regret scheduling").
  • Bands have byte/request limits and a TTL, so excess load is rejected early (HTTP 429/503) instead of timing out after minutes.

Production pattern: the API gateway strips client-supplied x-llm-d-* headers and injects authoritative tenant/objective headers from the authenticated API key or JWT.

What this lab does

Runs a quiet tenant (concurrency 4) and a noisy tenant (concurrency 384) concurrently, first through a plain EPP, then through an EPP with the flowControl feature gate (configs/epp/flow-control.yaml, adapted from upstream guides/flow-control).

Run it

cd llmd/lab03_flow_control && ./run_lab.sh

What to look for

  • quiet tenant ttft_p99_ms: large drop with flow control.
  • ALL throughput: about the same - flow control reorders work, it does not create capacity.
  • Tune maxConcurrency in the config: too high and nothing queues in the EPP; too low and replicas idle.

lessons.title: llm-d Lab 04: Tiered prefix cache (HBM -> CPU RAM -> storage)
lessons.html:
Concept

A B200 has 178 GB of HBM, but a node has ~2 TB of DRAM and tens of TB of NVMe. KV cache for Qwen3-32B costs ~256 KB per token (64 layers x 8 KV heads x 128 dim x 2 (K,V) x 2 bytes), so one 8K-token conversation is ~2 GB. A few hundred concurrent agentic sessions overflow HBM quickly.

Recomputing an evicted 8K prefix costs a full prefill (hundreds of ms on a busy replica). Copying 2 GB back from pinned host RAM over PCIe Gen5 / C2C takes tens of ms and doesn't use the GPU's compute. That is the whole idea of KV offloading:

Tier Typical size per node Who manages it
HBM (GPU) 100s of GB vLLM prefix cache / SGLang RadixAttention
CPU DRAM 1-2 TB vLLM OffloadingConnector (CPU tier), SGLang HiCache, LMCache

lessons.title: llm-d Lab 05: Prefill/decode (P/D) disaggregation
lessons.html:
Concept

Prefill and decode want different hardware behaviour:

Prefill Decode
Work per step thousands of tokens of one prompt one token for each of many sequences
Bottleneck tensor-core FLOPs (compute-bound) HBM bandwidth reading weights + KV (memory-bound)
Best parallelism low TP, many replicas higher TP / large batch
SLO it drives TTFT TPOT / ITL

In an aggregated server both phases share a GPU. Chunked prefill (vLLM lab 05) limits the damage, but every long prompt that arrives still steals step time from in-flight decodes, so TPOT jitters with prompt traffic.

Disaggregation runs them on separate pools:

  1. The router picks a prefill server (llm-d: prefix-cache-affinity-filter
    • token-load-scorer) and sends the request with max_tokens=1 and kv_transfer_params.do_remote_decode=true.
  2. The prefill server computes the KV cache, holds the blocks for a lease (kv_lease_duration), and returns kv_transfer_params (engine id, block ids, host, port).
  3. The router picks a decode server (llm-d: active-request-scorer) and sends the request with those params. The decoder pulls the blocks via NIXL (NixlConnector, UCX transport: NVLink cuda_ipc on a node, RDMA over InfiniBand/RoCE/EFA across nodes) and streams the output.

In llm-d the router schedules every request twice (once per pool) and a routing sidecar next to each decode pod runs the P-then-D protocol. Both pools are one InferencePool, deployed as a LeaderWorkerSet DisaggregatedSet so prefill and decode roll out as one version. The pools can use different TP sizes (NIXL supports heterogeneous TP) and scale independently.

What this lab does

Upstream reference topology on one node: openai/gpt-oss-120b, 1 prefill (TP=1) + 1 decode (TP=4). common/pd_proxy.py implements the router side of the protocol in ~100 lines so you can read it. Three runs with ~8K-token prompts: aggregated TP=4, P/D 1P1D, P/D 2P1D.

Run it

cd llmd/lab05_pd_disaggregation && ./run_lab.sh
IN_TOKENS=2000 ./run_lab.sh     # see where P/D stops paying off

What to look for

  • tpot_p50_ms lower/steadier with P/D, at the price of a transfer hop in TTFT.
  • Prefill-pool saturation in 1P1D and the fix in 2P1D: the "scale P and D independently" argument.
  • Decoder log lines about NIXL handshakes and transfers.
  • Kubernetes version of this lab: lab08 deploys the upstream pd-disaggregation guide unchanged.

lessons.title: llm-d Lab 06: Wide expert parallelism
lessons.html:
Concept

Mixture-of-Experts models (DeepSeek-V3/R1, Qwen3-MoE, gpt-oss, Kimi) replace each dense FFN with many experts, of which a router activates a few per token. DeepSeek-R1 has 671B parameters but only ~37B are active per token, so the model needs a lot of memory but relatively little compute per token.

How to spread it over GPUs:

  • Tensor parallelism (TP) slices every expert across all GPUs. Each expert's GEMM becomes tiny and every layer ends with an all-reduce.
  • Expert parallelism (EP) gives each GPU whole experts. Tokens are sent to the GPU that owns their expert (all-to-all dispatch) and the results come back (combine). Attention runs data-parallel (DP): each GPU processes its own batch of requests with a full copy of the attention weights.
  • Wide EP = EP across many GPUs and nodes (EP=32..96), so each GPU holds few experts and has HBM left over for a large KV cache and batch. All-to-all over NVLink + RDMA becomes the critical path. DeepEP kernels provide a high-throughput mode (prefill) and a low-latency, CUDA-graph-compatible mode (decode), which is why wide-EP is paired with P/D disaggregation.
  • EPLB (expert-parallel load balancing) replicates hot experts and rebalances placement periodically, because real traffic routes unevenly.

vLLM flags:

vllm serve <moe-model> --data-parallel-size 8 --enable-expert-parallel \
  [--all2all-backend deepep_low_latency] [--enable-eplb]
# EP size = TP x DP; without --enable-expert-parallel MoE layers use TP over TP x DP GPUs

llm-d's wide-ep guide: DeepSeek-R1-0528 on 32 H200, prefill DP16 + decode DP16 (2 nodes each), DeepEP + NIXL, deployed as a DisaggregatedSet of LeaderWorkerSets.

What this lab does

Single node, Qwen/Qwen3-30B-A3B: TP=8 vs DP=8+EP vs DP=8+EP+EPLB, at high concurrency.

Run it

cd llmd/lab06_wide_ep && ./run_lab.sh
CONCURRENCY=8 REQUESTS=64 ./run_lab.sh     # latency regime

What to look for

  • Throughput at high concurrency: DP+EP > TP.
  • Latency at low concurrency: TP can win.
  • EPLB: small gain on synthetic random tokens (expert routing is close to uniform); larger gains on real skewed traffic.

lessons.title: llm-d Lab 07: A Kubernetes cluster for llm-d on one 8xB200 node
lessons.html:
Concept: what Kubernetes adds

Labs 01-06 wired everything by hand: container names, ports, GPU indices, an endpoints file. That works on one box, but a production fleet needs:

  • Scheduling onto GPUs: the NVIDIA device plugin advertises nvidia.com/gpu as a node resource; pods request nvidia.com/gpu: 2 and the scheduler places them. (DRA, resource.k8s.io/v1, is the newer model for richer device claims.)
  • Self-healing and rollouts: Deployments/LeaderWorkerSets restart crashed replicas, probes gate traffic until the model is loaded, rollouts drain gracefully (--shutdown-timeout, preStop).
  • Service discovery: the EPP watches an InferencePool (pods selected by label) instead of a YAML file.
  • Multi-pod replicas: a LeaderWorkerSet (LWS) treats a group of pods (e.g. one model replica spanning 2 nodes) as one unit; a DisaggregatedSet bundles prefill and decode LWS roles so they roll out together.
  • Autoscaling: HPA/KEDA scale replicas on metrics (lab 09).

The llm-d guides are Kustomize-first for model servers (guides/<guide>/modelserver/<accelerator>/<engine>/<provider>/) and use Helm charts for the router (llm-d-router-standalone = EPP + Envoy sidecar; llm-d-router-gateway = EPP behind a Kubernetes Gateway). Requirements: Kubernetes 1.29+ (1.33+ recommended), helm 3.12+, kubectl, kustomize 5+, yq, helmfile.

What this lab does

  1. minikube start --driver docker --container-runtime docker --gpus all (single node, all 8 GPUs, $HF_HOME mounted at /var/cache/huggingface).
  2. Installs the shared CRDs/controllers: Gateway API Inference Extension, llm-d router CRDs (InferenceObjective), LeaderWorkerSet with DisaggregatedSet, KEDA.

Alternatives on bare metal: k3s or kubeadm + the NVIDIA GPU Operator. The guides themselves are cluster-agnostic (INFRA_PROVIDER=base).

Run it

cd llmd/lab00_setup && ./run_lab.sh --with-k8s-tools   # once
cd ../lab07_k8s_cluster && ./run_lab.sh
./run_lab.sh --delete                                   # when done

Prerequisite on the host: NVIDIA Container Toolkit configured for Docker (sudo nvidia-ctk runtime configure --runtime=docker && sudo systemctl restart docker).

lessons.title: llm-d Lab 08: The well-lit paths on Kubernetes
lessons.html:
Concept

llm-d packages its optimizations as well-lit paths: guides with tested manifests, a validated reference model/topology, and nightly end-to-end CI. Each guide is the same three steps (deploy_guide.sh does them for you):

# 1. router: EPP + Envoy sidecar, configured by layered Helm values
helm install <guide> oci://ghcr.io/llm-d/charts/llm-d-router-standalone \
  -f guides/recipes/router/base.values.yaml -f guides/<guide>/router/<guide>.values.yaml \
  -n llm-d-<guide> --version v0
# 2. model servers: Kustomize overlay per accelerator / engine / provider
kubectl apply -n llm-d-<guide> -k guides/<guide>/modelserver/gpu/vllm/base/
# 3. verify through the router Service (port 80 -> Envoy 8081)
Guide Reference topology (NVIDIA) What it adds
optimized-baseline Qwen3-32B, 2 replicas x TP=2 prefix-cache-affinity-filter + token-load-scorer; the default to start from.
precise-prefix-cache-routing same Model servers publish KV-cache events over ZMQ; the router's KV indexer knows exactly which blocks each pod holds. The router renders (tokenizes) each prompt to look it up.
tiered-prefix-cache same, 300 GiB CPU tier per pod vLLM OffloadingConnector (or SGLang HiCache / LMCache) plus a router scorer for the CPU tier.
pd-disaggregation gpt-oss-120b, 1P (TP=1) + 1D (TP=4) Prefill/decode pools in one DisaggregatedSet, NIXL KV transfer, router schedules each request twice.
predicted-latency-routing Qwen3-32B, 2 x TP=2 XGBoost sidecars trained online predict TTFT/TPOT per pod; optional SLO headers (x-llm-d-slo-ttft-ms).
flow-control Qwen3-32B Per-tenant fair queuing with priority bands (InferenceObjective).
wide-ep DeepSeek-R1, 32 GPUs DP+EP across nodes with DeepEP + P/D (multi-node; see lab 06 for the single-node version).

What this lab does

Deploys, load-tests and tears down (to free the GPUs) the guides above that fit on one 8xB200 node: optimized-baseline, precise-prefix-cache-routing, tiered-prefix-cache, pd-disaggregation, flow-control. Each guide gets a workload that shows off its feature. Per-pod vLLM counters are read through the API server proxy, the same way the guides' verification steps do.

Run it

cd llmd/lab08_k8s_well_lit_paths

KEEP=1 ./run_lab.sh precise-prefix-cache-routing # leave it running to explore
MODEL_SERVER=sglang ./deploy_guide.sh optimized-baseline   # SGLang pods instead

What to look for

  • *-pod-metrics.txt: requests and prefix hits concentrated per prefix group (optimized-baseline, precise), CPU-tier hits (tiered), prefill vs decode roles (P/D).
  • flow-control: premium tenant latency vs batch.
  • Compare against the Docker labs 01-05: same mechanisms, now with discovery, health probes, rollouts and Helm-managed config.
  • Calibration (guides/recipes/router/calibration) - the reference peakPrefillThroughput is for H100; measure it for B200.

lessons.title: llm-d Lab 09: Observability and SLO-aware autoscaling
lessons.html:
Concept

Why CPU/GPU utilization is the wrong autoscaling signal for LLMs. During continuous batching the GPU reports close to 100% utilization almost regardless of load, so utilization says nothing about whether users are waiting. By the time latency visibly degrades, requests are already queueing. Good signals are leading and inference-aware:

Signal Source Meaning
in-flight requests EPP (llm_d_epp_inflight_requests) demand currently in the system
flow-control queue size EPP (llm_d_epp_flow_control_queue_size) demand the pool cannot absorb right now
pool saturation EPP (llm_d_epp_flow_control_pool_saturation) fraction of capacity used
waiting requests / KV-cache usage vLLM (vllm:num_requests_waiting, vllm:kv_cache_usage_perc) per-replica pressure

llm-d's current autoscaling paths all use KEDA (the Workload Variant Autoscaler is deprecated): KEDA's Prometheus scaler queries one of the EPP metrics above, publishes it to the external metrics API, and the HPA that KEDA manages scales the model-server Deployment. KEDA can also scale to zero.

The startup problem. A new replica must pull a multi-GB image, load tens of GB of weights, compile, and capture CUDA graphs before serving, which can take minutes. Mitigations: node-local weight caches, pre-pulled images, the torch.compile cache, fast model actuation (keep a sleeping vLLM process with weights in CPU memory: /sleep and /wake_up), and scaling early on queue growth rather than late on latency.

Observability stack. Prometheus scrapes the EPP and every vLLM pod (ServiceMonitors/PodMonitors), Grafana shows the llm-d dashboards, and OpenTelemetry + Jaeger give per-request traces across Envoy → EPP → vLLM.

What this lab does

  1. Installs Prometheus + Grafana and the llm-d dashboards (upstream scripts).
  2. Deploys optimized-baseline with monitoring.
  3. Applies the upstream KEDA ScaledObject (keda-epp, in-flight signal).
  4. Starts at 1 replica, drives a heavy load ramp, records desired vs ready replicas every 10 s to replica_timeline.csv, then watches scale-down.

Run it

cd llmd/lab09_k8s_autoscaling_observability && ./run_lab.sh

What to look for

  • Lag between desired rising and ready rising (startup cost).
  • KEDA's currentMetrics vs the target value.
  • In Grafana: queueing at the EPP vs inside vLLM as replicas come up.

lessons.title: Regions, DNS and global traffic
lessons.html:
Building blocks

  • Region: a geographic area (e.g. us-east, eu-west) with several availability zones (AZs): independent datacenters with separate power and networking, a few ms apart. Spread replicas across AZs to survive a datacenter failure; across regions to survive a regional outage and to be close to users.
  • Latency floor: light in fiber covers ~200 km per ms, so a round trip New York ↔ Frankfurt (~6,200 km) is ≥ 60 ms, and real paths are ~80-90 ms. For a chatbot that's noise compared to prefill; for voice agents and tool loops with dozens of round trips it adds up. Put inference near users, or at least near the systems that call it.
  • GPU geography: GPU capacity is unevenly distributed across regions and clouds, so "near the user" competes with "where the GPUs are". Many deployments serve from a few GPU-rich regions and route globally.

Getting users to a region

  1. DNS: the client resolves api.example.com. GeoDNS / latency-based DNS returns the IP of the nearest healthy region; health checks remove failed regions. Caveat: DNS answers are cached for the record TTL (keep it short, 30-60 s, for failover) and resolvers may be far from users.
  2. Anycast: the same IP is announced via BGP from many locations; the internet routes each client to the topologically nearest one. Global load balancers and CDNs use anycast front ends that terminate TLS at the edge and forward over the provider's backbone.
  3. Edge / CDN: points of presence close to users terminate TCP+TLS (saving round trips), apply WAF/DDoS protection, and keep long-lived connections to origin regions. LLM responses aren't cacheable like images, but edge termination still cuts the connection-setup latency and protects the origin. Streaming (SSE) must pass through without buffering.
user ─► DNS (GeoDNS) ─► anycast edge PoP (TLS, WAF, DDoS) ─► provider backbone
     ─► regional L7 load balancer / API gateway ─► inference cluster (llm-d router) ─► GPUs

Routing policy across regions

  • Latency-based: nearest region by measured RTT.
  • Weighted: split traffic (e.g. 90/10 for a canary region).
  • Failover: primary/secondary with health checks.
  • Capacity-aware: send overflow to regions with spare GPUs (needs a global view of queue depth or saturation - the same signals the llm-d EPP uses inside a cluster, aggregated up).
  • Data residency: EU users' prompts must stay in EU regions (GDPR, customer contracts), which overrides latency.

Multi-region active-active

Each region runs a full stack (gateway, router, model servers) and serves live traffic. Requirements: identical model versions everywhere (artifact registry replication), configuration as code, per-region capacity for failover (N+1: if one region of N fails, the rest absorb its load), and state that is either regional (conversation KV caches are regional and rebuildable) or replicated (user accounts, quotas).

lessons.title: Load balancers, API gateways and admission control
lessons.html:
L4 vs L7

  • L4 (transport) load balancers forward TCP/UDP connections by IP/port. Fast and simple, but one long-lived HTTP/2 connection carrying thousands of requests lands on one backend.
  • L7 (application) load balancers / proxies (Envoy, NGINX, cloud ALBs) parse HTTP, so they can route per request, by path or header, retry, apply timeouts, and terminate TLS. Classic policies: round-robin, least-request, consistent hashing (session affinity).
  • Inference-aware L7 (llm-d EPP via Envoy ext_proc, Gateway API Inference Extension) adds model-server state: queue depth, KV-cache usage, prefix-cache locality, predicted latency, P/D roles, LoRA adapters loaded. llm-d lab 01 shows why this beats round-robin and least-request.

The API gateway layer

In front of the inference router, a production API usually has an API gateway that does what the GPUs shouldn't:

Concern How
Authentication API keys, OAuth/JWT validation, mTLS for service-to-service
Tenant identity derive tenant/tier from the token, strip client-supplied x-llm-d-* headers, inject authoritative x-llm-d-inference-fairness-id / x-llm-d-inference-objective
Rate limiting requests/min and tokens/min per key (token-bucket); prompt tokens can be counted up front, output tokens charged as they stream
Quotas & billing per-tenant token accounting, usage events to a billing pipeline
Model routing map public model names to pools/versions, A/B and canary splits
Safety input/output moderation, PII filtering, prompt-injection defenses
Observability request ids, traces (W3C traceparent), access logs

Admission control and backpressure

Accepting more work than you can serve only converts overload into timeouts. Layers of defense:

  1. Gateway rate limits per tenant (protects everyone from one tenant).
  2. Router flow control (llm-d lab 03): per-tenant fair queues with priorities; hold requests in the router while the pool is saturated; reject (429) when a band's queue or TTL limits are hit.
  3. Engine limits: --max-num-seqs, --max-num-batched-tokens, preemption when KV runs out.
  4. Client behavior: retries with exponential backoff and jitter, and respecting Retry-After; otherwise retry storms amplify overload.

Shedding low-priority (batch, best-effort) traffic first keeps interactive latency within SLO during spikes.

Streaming through proxies

Every proxy on the path must stream SSE without buffering, allow long request durations (minutes for long generations), and propagate client disconnects so the engine can abort the request and free its KV cache.

lessons.title: GPU capacity, autoscaling and cost
lessons.html:
Capacity planning from first principles

  1. Traffic model: peak requests/s, input and output token distributions, prefix reuse, diurnal pattern per region.
  2. Per-replica capacity at SLO: from benchmarks (the labs), the maximum requests/s one replica sustains while meeting p99 TTFT and TPOT targets - goodput, not peak throughput.
  3. Replicas = peak load / per-replica goodput, plus headroom for failures (N+1 per AZ/region) and deploys.
  4. Memory check: weights + KV for the concurrency implied by Little's law (concurrency = rate × latency) must fit, per replica.

Cost per million tokens

cost per 1M output tokens = (GPU $/hour × GPUs) ÷ (output tokens/s × 3600) × 1,000,000

Illustrative: 8 GPUs at $5/GPU-hour = $40/h. At 20,000 output tokens/s sustained that is 72M tokens/h → ≈ $0.56 per 1M output tokens. At 30% average utilization the effective cost is ~3x higher. Every optimization in the engine labs moves this number: FP8 (~1.5-2x tokens/s), prefix caching (fewer prefill FLOPs), speculative decoding (lower latency at low load), and routing (higher cache hit rates per GPU).

Input tokens are cheaper than output tokens (prefill is parallel and compute-efficient), which is why providers price them separately and why cached input tokens are discounted further.

Buying GPUs

Option Trade-off
On-demand flexible, most expensive, may be unavailable for large GPUs
Reservations / committed use cheaper per hour, you pay whether used or not
Spot / preemptible cheapest, can be reclaimed with short notice: batch and offline inference
Multi-cloud / neoclouds more capacity, more operational surface

Common pattern: reserved capacity for the baseline, on-demand or another region for peaks, spot for batch jobs (llm-d's batch gateway / async processing fits here).

Autoscaling LLM services

  • Scale on leading signals: router in-flight requests, queue size, pool saturation, KV-cache pressure - not GPU utilization, which reads ~100% under any batching load (llm-d lab 09).
  • Startup latency dominates: image pull + weight load + compile + CUDA graph capture can take minutes. Mitigations: pre-pulled images, weights on node-local NVMe or a fast distributed cache, compile caches, model streaming loaders, sleep/wake (fast model actuation: keep a vLLM process with weights parked in host memory, wake in seconds).
  • Scale-down carefully: drain in-flight requests (--shutdown-timeout, preStop hooks); scaling a pool with warm prefix caches down loses those caches.
  • Cluster autoscaler / node provisioning adds GPU nodes when pods are pending; for GPUs this can take many minutes, so keep warm spare nodes for bursty traffic.
  • Scale to zero suits rarely used models (KEDA), at the cost of a cold start on the first request.

Multi-model and multi-tenant efficiency

  • LoRA adapters: serve many fine-tunes on one base model; the router can prefer replicas with the adapter loaded.
  • Model variants across accelerator types (H100, B200, MI355X) with the router picking the cheapest pool that meets the SLO.
  • Priority tiers: interactive traffic first, batch fills the gaps.

lessons.title: Reliability, rollouts and observability
lessons.html:
SLOs and error budgets

  • SLI (indicator): a measured ratio, e.g. "fraction of requests with TTFT < 1 s and no 5xx".
  • SLO (objective): the target, e.g. 99.5% over 28 days.
  • Error budget: 1 − SLO = 0.5% of requests may miss. While budget remains, ship features; when it's burning fast, freeze risky changes and fix reliability. Alert on burn rate (budget consumed per hour), not on single blips.

For LLM APIs, define separate SLOs for availability (non-5xx), TTFT and TPOT, per tier (interactive vs batch).

Failure modes specific to LLM serving

Failure Symptom Mitigation
GPU Xid / ECC / NVLink errors pod crash, NCCL hang health checks, node auto-repair, LWS group restart
KV cache exhaustion preemptions, TTFT spikes admission control, KV offload, more replicas
Hot prefix / hot tenant one replica saturated load-aware scoring (not pure affinity), flow control
Slow cold starts autoscale too late warm pools, sleep/wake, scale on queue signals
Model/tokenizer mismatch garbage output, failed tool parsing pinned images and artifacts, canaries with eval checks
Retry storms load doubles under failure backoff + jitter, retry budgets, 429 with Retry-After
Long requests during deploy dropped streams graceful drain (--shutdown-timeout, preStop), connection draining

Safe rollouts

  • Rolling update: replace pods a few at a time; readiness probes gate traffic.
  • Blue/green: stand up the new version beside the old, switch traffic, keep the old one for instant rollback.
  • Canary: send 1-5% of traffic (weighted HTTPRoute, gateway split) to the new model/engine version and compare SLIs and quality metrics (eval scores, refusal rates, tool-call parse errors) before ramping.
  • Shadow traffic: mirror requests to the new version without returning its responses, to measure performance safely.
  • Treat model weights, chat templates, engine version and flags as one versioned artifact - a change in any of them is a deploy.

Observability

  • Metrics (Prometheus): engine metrics (vllm:num_requests_running, vllm:num_requests_waiting, vllm:kv_cache_usage_perc, vllm:prefix_cache_hits_total, TTFT/ITL histograms), router metrics (EPP in-flight, flow-control queues, scheduling decisions), GPU metrics (DCGM exporter: SM activity, memory, power, Xid errors), gateway metrics.
  • Logs: structured, sampled; never log prompts by default (privacy).
  • Traces (OpenTelemetry → Jaeger/Tempo): one trace per request across gateway → Envoy → EPP → model server shows where time went (queueing vs prefill vs decode vs network).
  • Dashboards per layer and an SLO dashboard; llm-d ships Grafana dashboards for the router and model servers.

Disaster recovery

Define RTO (how fast you must recover) and RPO (how much data you may lose). Inference is mostly stateless, so DR is about capacity and artifacts: model weights replicated to every region's registry, infra as code to rebuild a cluster, tested regional failover (game days), and enough quota in the fallback regions.

lessons.title: Security, privacy and multi-tenancy
lessons.html:
Threats to an LLM service

  • Abuse: credential stuffing, scraping, denial of wallet (expensive long prompts), DDoS. → WAF/DDoS at the edge, auth, token-based rate limits.
  • Tenant isolation failures: one tenant seeing another's data. Shared prefix caches are safe in content terms (a cache hit requires the exact same tokens) but can leak timing (a fast TTFT reveals that someone sent that prefix). Mitigations: per-tenant cache salting/namespaces for sensitive tenants, dedicated pools for regulated customers.
  • Prompt injection / tool abuse: untrusted content steering an agent to call tools. → least-privilege tools, output validation, human approval for risky actions. (Structured outputs help parsing, not trust.)
  • Supply chain: malicious model files (pickle), compromised images or Python packages. → safetensors only, signed and scanned images, pinned digests, private registries and model mirrors.
  • Secrets: HF tokens, API keys in env vars or logs. → secret managers, Kubernetes Secrets with RBAC, never in images or command lines.

Data handling

  • Encrypt in transit (TLS at the edge, mTLS inside the mesh) and at rest (model registry, logs, KV offload tiers on disk).
  • Minimize retention: don't log prompts/responses by default; if you must (debugging, abuse review), redact PII and set short retention.
  • Data residency: keep prompts, logs and KV tiers in the user's region; route by geography at DNS/gateway level.
  • Offloaded KV on shared filesystems is user data - apply the same access controls and encryption as any other data store.

Network and cluster hygiene

  • Model servers and the EPP should not be reachable from the internet; only the gateway is. Use NetworkPolicies so only the router can reach model pods, and only the EPP can scrape them.
  • RBAC: the EPP only needs to watch pods/InferencePools in its namespace.
  • Run containers as non-root where possible; restrict privileged mounts (RDMA devices, host paths) to the pods that need them.

lessons.title: The life of one request
lessons.html:
A user in Berlin sends a chat message to api.example.com. Here is every hop, what it costs, and which lab or module covers it.

 ① DNS          ② Edge PoP          ③ Regional gateway      ④ llm-d router          ⑤ Model server         ⑥ GPU
 GeoDNS ──► anycast TLS/WAF ──► auth, quotas, tenant ──► Envoy + EPP pick ──► vLLM/SGLang schedule ──► prefill, decode
   ~10 ms*      ~5-20 ms           ~1-5 ms                 ~1-3 ms                queue: 0 .. seconds     ms .. seconds
                                                                                    ◄──── tokens stream back over SSE ────

* cached DNS answers cost ~0.

  1. DNS (Cloud 1). GeoDNS answers with the anycast IP of the global load balancer; the EU region is chosen for latency and data residency.
  2. Edge (Cloud 1). The nearest PoP terminates TCP+TLS (saving ~2 round trips to the origin), applies WAF/DDoS rules, and forwards over the provider backbone to eu-west.
  3. API gateway (Cloud 2, 5). Validates the API key/JWT, looks up the tenant (tier: premium), checks token-rate limits, strips any client x-llm-d-* headers and injects x-llm-d-inference-fairness-id: acme and x-llm-d-inference-objective: premium-traffic, starts a trace, maps model chat-large → InferencePool qwen3-32b-prod.
  4. llm-d router (llm-d labs 01-03). Envoy receives the request and streams it to the EPP over ext_proc. The EPP:
    • classifies the flow (tenant + priority) and, if the pool is saturated, queues it fairly (flow control);
    • hashes the prompt's blocks: the 3,000-token system prompt of this app is cached on replicas 3 and 7 (prefix-cache affinity);
    • filters to those, scores by queued prompt tokens (token load), picks replica 7, and returns x-gateway-destination-endpoint: 10.4.2.17:8000. In P/D mode it picks a prefill pod and a decode pod instead (llm-d lab 05).
  5. Model server (vLLM/SGLang labs). The API server applies the chat template and tokenizes. The scheduler admits the request into the next continuous batch if KV blocks are available (else it waits or preempts). Prefix caching finds 3,000 tokens already cached; only the new 150 tokens are prefilled (chunked so running decodes aren't stalled).
  6. GPU (Foundations 1-5). Prefill runs compute-bound GEMMs and FlashAttention-4 kernels; then each decode step streams all weights (FP8: half the bytes) plus this sequence's KV from HBM, inside a captured CUDA graph, verifying 3 EAGLE-3 draft tokens per step when acceptance is high.
  7. Streaming back. Each detokenized chunk is sent as an SSE event through Envoy, the gateway and the edge. The gateway counts output tokens for billing; the trace records TTFT and TPOT per hop.
  8. After the response. The KV blocks stay in the prefix cache (and are offloaded to CPU RAM when evicted) so the user's next turn hits the cache
    • as long as the router sends it back to replica 7 or its CPU tier.

Where the latency goes (typical 32B model, warm cache)

Component Budget
Network to region (TLS at edge) 20-60 ms
Gateway + router 2-8 ms
Queueing 0 ms at healthy load; seconds when overloaded
Prefill 150 new tokens (3K cached) ~20-40 ms
Prefill 3K tokens uncached ~150-300 ms
Decode, per token 10-30 ms

The single biggest lever on TTFT is usually not recomputing the prefix (cache + cache-aware routing); on TPOT it is bytes per step (precision, batch, speculation); on tail latency it is queueing (capacity, flow control, autoscaling).

lessons.title: Reference architecture for a global LLM service
lessons.html:
┌──────────────────────── Global ────────────────────────┐
  clients ─► GeoDNS ─► anycast edge (TLS, WAF, DDoS) ─► global LB (latency/geo/capacity)
                           └───────────────┬──────────────────────┬─────────────────┘
                                           ▼                      ▼
            ┌────────────── Region us-east ──────────┐   ┌──── Region eu-west ────┐
            │ API gateway: authn, quotas, tenant hdrs│   │ (same stack; EU data   │
            │ model routing, moderation, metering    │   │  stays in EU)          │
            │                   │                    │   └────────────────────────┘
            │   ┌───────── Kubernetes cluster(s) ─────────────────────────┐      │
            │   │ llm-d router (Envoy + EPP, 2+ replicas, HA)              │      │
            │   │   flow control → filters → scorers → picker              │      │
            │   │ InferencePool A: Qwen3-32B FP8, aggregated, TP=2 × N     │      │
            │   │ InferencePool B: DeepSeek MoE, P/D + wide-EP (LWS)       │      │
            │   │ KV tiers: HBM → CPU RAM → NVMe/shared FS                  │      │
            │   │ KEDA autoscaling on EPP metrics; warm/sleeping replicas  │      │
            │   └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘      │
            │ Model registry mirror · image registry · secrets manager           │
            │ Prometheus/Grafana · OTel traces · logs · SLO alerts               │
            └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
  Control plane: GitOps (Helm/Kustomize) · CI with perf + eval gates · canary controller

Layer responsibilities

Layer Owns Course
Global traffic DNS, anycast, edge TLS, region selection, failover Cloud 1
Gateway identity, quotas, tenant/priority headers, model mapping, safety, billing Cloud 2, 5
Inference router (llm-d) replica choice (cache/load/latency aware), P/D scheduling, fair queuing, pool discovery llm-d 01-05, 08
Model server (vLLM/SGLang) batching, KV paging and caching, kernels, quantization, speculation, parallelism vLLM & SGLang tracks
Accelerators HBM, tensor cores, NVLink, RDMA NICs Foundations 1-3
Platform Kubernetes, LWS, GPU operators, autoscaling, observability, rollouts Foundations 7, llm-d 07-09, Cloud 3-4

Design decisions and defaults

  • Engine: vLLM for breadth of models, hardware and features; SGLang for RadixAttention-heavy workloads, structured generation and some MoE/DeepSeek optimizations. llm-d supports both behind the same router.
  • Precision: BF16 to validate, then FP8 (W8A8 + FP8 KV) as the production default on Hopper/Blackwell; FP4 (NVFP4/MXFP4) where evals allow.
  • Topology: smallest TP that fits with KV headroom; DP replicas behind the llm-d optimized baseline. Add P/D when prompts are long and TPOT SLOs strict; wide-EP for large MoE models across nodes.
  • Caching: prefix caching always on; cache-aware routing; CPU KV tier for multi-turn/agentic traffic; precise prefix routing when the pool is large.
  • Admission: gateway rate limits + router flow control with priority bands; batch traffic as best-effort or through a batch API.
  • Scaling: KEDA on EPP queue/saturation signals; warm capacity sized to startup time × growth rate.
  • Release safety: perf and eval gates in CI; canaries per region; model, template, engine and flags versioned together.

lessons.title: The optimization playbook
lessons.html:
A checklist that maps symptoms to the lab that fixes them.

Single replica (vLLM / SGLang)

Symptom Likely cause Try Lab
Very low tokens/s, GPU underused FP32 or naive HF loop, static batching BF16, a real engine with continuous batching vLLM 00-02, SGLang 01-02
Few concurrent sequences fit KV cache too big FP8 KV, GQA model, smaller max-model-len, more GPUs vLLM 08, Foundations 2
High TTFT with shared system prompts prefix recomputation prefix caching / RadixAttention vLLM 04, SGLang 05
TPOT spikes when long prompts arrive prefill interrupting decode chunked prefill, tune max-num-batched-tokens; later P/D vLLM 05, SGLang 06, llm-d 05
Slow decode at low concurrency launch overhead, eager mode CUDA graphs, -O2, overlap scheduling vLLM 06, SGLang 07
Slow decode at low concurrency, graphs on memory-bound weights FP8/MXFP8/FP4 or INT4 weights; speculative decoding vLLM 07-09, SGLang 03, 08
Long-prompt prefill slow attention kernel FA4 / FlashInfer / TRT-LLM backends vLLM 03, SGLang 12
Model doesn't fit / latency too high single-GPU limits tensor parallelism (inside NVLink) vLLM 10, SGLang 04
MoE model inefficient TP slicing experts DP attention + expert parallelism, EPLB SGLang 10, llm-d 06
JSON outputs invalid unconstrained sampling structured outputs (grammar backends) SGLang 09

Fleet (llm-d)

Symptom Try Lab
Prefix hit rate low despite shared prompts prefix-cache-aware routing llm-d 01
One replica hot, others idle load-aware scorers with affinity, calibrate peakPrefillThroughput llm-d 02
One tenant's burst hurts everyone flow control with fairness + priorities llm-d 03
Multi-turn sessions miss cache after a while CPU/NVMe KV tier + tier-aware routing llm-d 04, SGLang 13
Approximate cache routing mispredicts at scale precise prefix-cache routing (KV events) llm-d 08
Long prompts + strict TPOT P/D disaggregation, scale P and D separately llm-d 05, 08
Big MoE across nodes wide-EP with DeepEP + P/D llm-d 06
Latency SLOs differ per request predicted-latency routing with SLO headers llm-d 08
Capacity lags demand KEDA on EPP signals, warm pools, sleep/wake llm-d 09

Order of operations

  1. Measure a baseline with the target workload shape (lengths, prefix reuse), not just random tokens.
  2. Get the engine basics right: BF16 → FP8, prefix caching, chunked prefill, CUDA graphs, right TP.
  3. Scale out with DP replicas behind an inference-aware router.
  4. Add the specialised paths only when their symptom shows up: P/D, KV tiers, wide-EP, flow control, predicted latency.
  5. Re-measure after each change, including quality.
